en: The Buddha Spoke the Scripture on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footing, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, staying beneath a Pāṭali tree.

Upon a stone of deep blue lapis lazuli, the Buddha sat and preached the Dharma for his mother throughout the three months of the summer retreat. He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus; eight thousand bhikṣus had all attained arhatship, their defilements were exhausted, they were fully endowed with supernormal powers, and they were capable of performing all manner of deeds.

There were also seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas who had mastered spiritual penetrations and attained dharanis; they knew the thoughts and desires of all people’s minds and traveled freely to countless buddha-fields.
At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of followers as he preached the Dharma.
Among the assembly of devas, there were two sons of gods:
one named Candradeva and the other named Candratārakadeva, who were seated within the gathering.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Candra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha while kneeling:
"If you would grant me the opportunity to speak, I now wish to ask a question."
The Buddha said,
"Ask whatever you wish. Thereupon,
the Devaputra Candra leaped for joy and spoke a verse to question the Buddha:
"Out of great compassion for all, he is pure, profound, and beneficial;
having established them in the attainment of the Way, he most purely bestows the nectar of immortality.
Having already attained peace for himself, he has extinguished and eliminated all defilements."
Furthermore, you are able to bring peace to all; for this reason, I wish to ask:
throughout incalculable eons, your practice was exceedingly diligent and arduous;
you relinquished everything you possessed, giving in charity without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
With a mind of universal equanimity, I feel equal compassion for all people;
Now, for this reason, I wish to question the Honored One among men!
Those who behold the Buddha’s body, Adorned with its manifold marks of excellence;
All have given rise to a heart of exultation, Attaining this through the field of merit.
Vast and long, it is without limit, Immeasurable and exceeding the great ocean;
Therefore, I now wish to inquire Of him whose virtue is unsurpassed.
He has no divergent intent, nor does he have a divergent mind;
the Hero among those who lead the three realms thoroughly understands all thoughts.
Regarding the conduct appropriate for his own body, he has never followed others.
Therefore, I now wish to ask the Great Wise One of the world:
regarding those with virtue and those without virtue, praise and slander;
having a name and being nameless; and suffering as well as happiness—[how does one regard these]?
All know the eight worldly concerns and have understood them through discernment;
therefore, I wish to ask you, who are already free from all fears.
You protect all people while maintaining yourself without distinction.
Thus there is neither increase nor decrease; such is the nature of all three realms!
Having compassion for others, being free from doubt and free from malice;
therefore I wish to ask: you uphold your conduct like the earth.
In practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts, their minds are exceedingly pure;
they would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than ever violate the precepts.
Just as they act with body and speech, so too is it with their mind!
Therefore, I wish to ask one who has transcended the world:
how does one practice patience to discipline the mind, remaining steadfast while diminishing the self?
All these are the deeds of wisdom, for they perceive the places of diligent suffering.
All things, whether good or evil, and all instances of anger, you are able to endure;
for this reason I wish to ask you, for all that was to be done has been accomplished.
Your power of diligence is exceedingly strong, surpassing all debate.
For the sake of the world you undergo toil and hardship, never for your own person;
day and night you constantly persevere in seeking [the truth], like a swift river flowing into the sea.
Therefore I wish to ask: how do your virtues compare to those of the heavens?
Thus, regarding all matters of desire, he no longer acts within the three realms;
all forms of affection and attachment he has completely subdued.
He is fully endowed with the dhyānas and the pāramitās, and his supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) are likewise perfected.
Therefore, I wish to ask the Hero among Men,
who possesses great wisdom and has already crossed over to where there is nothing to delight in;
he has completely abandoned all evil deeds throughout kalpa after kalpa.
If one dwells in seclusion, they will know all dharmas with mastery; therefore,
I wish to ask about that which distinguishes the spiritual from the mundane—
the wisdom of the power of the divine feet that extinguishes all that is unwholesome.
From here he travels to other lands, yet does not harbor thoughts of praising himself;
he makes offerings to all Buddhas, yet maintains no conceptualization of the Buddhas.
For this reason, I wish to ask: O Compassionate One, please manifest yourself for the sake of the world.
At that time, all the Māras came and gathered together in a great assembly;
yet by the power of the Way, all the Māras were spontaneously defeated.
Having thus subdued the Māras, he personally attained the realization of the Way.
Therefore, I wish to ask: his merit is most supreme.
All those dwelling upon the earth, from their golden seats, sprang forth from the ground;
they immediately attained the path of awakening—the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable.
I have arisen and gone elsewhere, having fully understood all doctrines;
therefore, I wish to inquire of the Most Supreme among Men,
whose merit of omniscience makes him the Honored One among the honored!
Having already attained the intent of the Buddhas, he preaches and practices the Dharma accordingly.
Having gathered [the assembly], he brings them to liberation;
for the sake of all beings, the Teacher asks about this matter, so that those within the three realms may all receive his grace.
Thereupon, having praised the Buddha with these verses, the Moon Devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain the sustaining power of the great supernormal knowledge and wisdom, thereby achieving the most supreme *pāramitā*?"
How does a bodhisattva attain inconceivable skillful means and come to know the deliberations in the minds of others?
How does a bodhisattva come to know all dharmas as being of a single practice, a single flavor, a single entrance, and a single teaching?
How does one attain wisdom such that one may teach others with full confidence?
How does a bodhisattva attain profound precepts, act without negligence, and personally realize the unsurpassed, true, and correct path without ever being separated from the Buddha?
"Such is what I have asked,
World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain it for me."
The Buddha told the Devaputra Candra:
“Excellent, excellent,
Devaputra!
One who desires to practice the deeds of a Tathāgata;
one who desires to don the great armor of saṃnāha-saṃnaddha;
one who desires to enter the great battle as a great leader.
Desiring to deliver all beings;
desiring to become a great ship;
desiring to turn the great wheel of Dharma.
Desiring to perform great giving;
desiring to manifest the great Dharma-body;
desiring to bring forth the great rain of Dharma;
Desiring to kindle the great fire of the Dharma;
desiring to beat the great drum of the Dharma;
desiring to raise the great banner of the Dharma;
Desiring to expound the Great Dharma-realm;
desiring to emit the Great Dharma-sound;
desiring to cultivate the Great Dharma-fragrance;
Desiring to manifest the wisdom of the Great Dharma;
desiring to sever the sacrifices of false views;
and desiring to establish and fulfill the Great Sacrifice—wishing thus to perform such inconceivable deeds for the sake of all beings—he maintains this deliberation and asks the Tathāgata about it.
The Buddha said to the devaputra:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!"
I shall explain this for you.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain great wisdom and reach the most profound and subtle precepts, they personally realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Listen to what the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has spoken.
Thereupon, the Moon Devaputra, together with the great assembly, joined his palms in reverence and listened to the instruction.
The Buddha said to the devaputra:
"A bodhisattva has four dharmas by which they attain the foremost, distinguished, and great supernormal power-holding.
What are these four?
First, knowing that the characteristics of all phenomena neither increase nor decrease;
second, seeking and investigating all phenomena;
third, realizing that all phenomena are inexhaustible, attaining meditative concentration and peace, and achieving the realization of training.
Fourth, not perceiving any phenomena as being apart from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one does not harbor expectations toward or conceptualize any other realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
These are the four matters.
"How, O Devaputra, does one know the characteristics of dharmas?
One knows that the past is empty, the future is empty, and the present is also empty; all that exists is likewise empty, just like space."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
To sit long in samādhi seeking emptiness, yet each not knowing its location—this is called "thoroughly understanding.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
To know these points is called analytical discernment (*vibhāga-pravicaya*).

Having thoroughly understood all determinations, one maintains them and transmits them by teaching others these points: the point of knowing, the point of establishing, the point of differentiation, the point of suchness, and the point of resolving through discussion; this successive transmission is called merit (*guṇa*).
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
How does one attain all dharmas?
The dharma does not conceive of a self, nor does the self conceive of the dharma; when a dharma arises, it arises; when a dharma abides, it abides."
"O Son of Heaven!

All dharmas are thus: they are neither 'mine' nor 'not mine. For one who has already realized this regarding a bodhisattva, there is no further turning forward; for one who does not turn forward, there is no longer any delight in the place of arising and ceasing."
Why is this so? Because all that exists is non-existent.
When one contemplates other dharmas within that which is non-existent, although one contemplates them, there is nothing to be learned regarding those other dharmas.
Nor does one have anything to say;
nor does one abide anywhere. Although one brings great illumination to other dharmas, regarding these dharmas, one neither acts nor studies.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!"
"How does a bodhisattva come to know that all phenomena are equal to space?
O Devaputra, the mind constructs the three realms; it is thus, O Devaputra!"
The mind has no form and cannot be seen; it has no place of abiding and cannot be known. This mind and its mental phenomena are like an illusion; even when one seeks the mind, it cannot be found.
Thus, regarding the mind and mental factors, when one seeks the mind, it is utterly unobtainable; this mind is furthermore unknowable, and in this way, all phenomena are likewise unobtainable.

Furthermore, they cannot be grasped; phenomena are ultimately non-existent. One views all that exists as being truly like an illusion or a shadow. Having thus known all phenomena to be transcended, one who has transcended them spontaneously knows all things without further study. Thus one knows that all phenomena are equal to empty space.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Just as space cannot be seen, has no arising, and has no end, know that all dharmas are likewise!"
"Just as this space is likewise empty, tranquil, and pure, so too are all phenomena tranquil and pure.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
How does a bodhisattva come to know the dharma-nature of all phenomena?"
In this way, O Devaputra!
When a bodhisattva trains thus, they neither perceive nor can they apprehend any dharmas.
The eye does not see the ear, and the ear does not know the ear; the ear does not see the eye, and the eye does not know the eye.
The nose does not see the tongue, and the tongue does not know the tongue; the tongue does not see the nose, and the nose does not know the nose.
The nose does not see the body, and the body does not know the body; the body does not see the mind, and the mind does not know the mind.
Regarding all phenomena, whether they are in motion or at rest, how should one equally know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it abides?

Thus, when seeing and knowing phenomena through the eye and making distinctions among them, one neither says "it is" nor "it is not," nor does one follow after them; for this reason, one knows the place of eternal abiding, and one does not cause the decline of phenomena.
Why is this? Because externally there is no entering and internally there is no receiving; one should thus know and thus see that which is subject to decay and that which is not.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to anything nor abide in anything regarding phenomena; to abide in such a manner is to see all.
Thus it is, O Devaputra! This is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Such a nature of phenomena neither arises nor ceases; in this state there is nothing whatsoever, yet all phenomena are nevertheless manifested. Because it abides in the unborn and the unarisen, it is the place of cessation. To be thus discerning and truthful is like what is seen by the eye; wisdom is likewise so.

Nor does one dwell upon the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), nor is there anything to be liberated; yet one flourishes and abides therein, for those phenomena are fully perfected within their own nature.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
These are the four dharmas.
By attaining these, a bodhisattva gains the sustaining power of great supernormal knowledge and wisdom, and achieves the supreme perfection.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
"What are supernormal powers?
What is wisdom?
O Son of Heaven!"
As for "supernatural powers" (abhijñā):
one thoroughly knows the essential meaning of all dharmas and fully comprehends each and every aspect of that knowledge;
therefore, O Devaputra, it is called supernatural power.
"Regarding all dharmas, one knows oneself and one's own name, O Devaputra!
That the self is not stubborn—this is skill in the Dharma.
Thus it is, Devaputra!"
Because of this, the bodhisattva swiftly attains the mastery of great supernormal powers and remains insatiable in his wisdom regarding his vows. Why is this?
It is because he desires to fulfill those vows.

Such wisdom, O Devaputra, transcends the human eye and attains the purity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); it sees all the incalculable, boundless billions of Buddha-fields in the ten directions, and within those fields, it beholds the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their assemblies of disciples.
With the divine ear, it hears all that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach, and understands it all completely.

Within all Buddha-fields, they fully understand everything concerning the people—whether learned or unlearned, and matters of superior, middling, or inferior capacity. They are able to maintain their supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) to travel everywhere throughout the Buddha-fields. They know all that occurred during incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) in past lives; they know the thoughts in the minds of all people and the origins from which they come. They fully comprehend the beginning and end of their births, and by relying on this wisdom for self-realization, they are then able to preach the Dharma for all.
"By such wisdom, O Son of Heaven!

the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains all-knowledge (sarvajñatā); he abides in all that is performed by a Buddha, swiftly attains all Buddha-dharmas, and accomplishes the unsurpassed, right, true path of supreme perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"In this, his great supernormal powers are all fully perfected;
The application of his skillful means Is seen as the marks of merit."
Thus, all [arise] from this one; one fully understands all phenomena.
The virtue of profound and pure precepts is likewise attained through this.
For this reason, one comes to know all phenomena.
Ultimately, one does not practice within this [world], nor does one harbor thoughts that exceed or transgress it.
All things that exist—every dharma—is likewise so!
It is like empty space; the meaning of the Dharma is without distinction.
Thus, by scrutinizing the Dharma, one then attains the vision of the Dharma;
by no longer doubting the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), one understands it through clear realization.
It is not by merely adhering to the Dharma that one comes to possess complete knowledge.
Discerning and clearly understanding this, one personally attains supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
All phenomena of the past are entirely like empty space;
all phenomena of the future likewise do not exist.
All present phenomena now, / Are likewise entirely like space;
/ Those who see them thus / See all things as equal.
/ These phenomena of the three times / Are all entirely like empty space.
Neither is it mine, nor is it not mine; having known this for oneself regarding one life, all things are likewise so!
When one perceives all such things in this way, one attains transformative faith.
Knowing thus regarding those things, their merits are no longer the same;
they preach the Dharma for the sake of all, yet do not form conceptual attachments to that Dharma.
They are free from resentment and harbor no talk of right or wrong.
There is nothing to be doubted, nor is there anything to be perceived.
For one who has become thus, all dharmas are established;
therein, whatever is practiced is entirely without remainder.
Thus there is no remaining phenomenon; all phenomena are exactly like this!
Nor does one perceive anything further within a different phenomenon.
In this way, they do not arise, nor do they come into being again.
Thus there is nowhere to enter, nor is there anything to be attained.
Having thereby realized virtue, one preaches the Dharma for all;
universally expounding the meaning of the Dharma, one has no conceptual thoughts regarding the Path.
That mind, within the three realms, is already exceedingly excellent and joyful;
yet when the mind is thus, it is entirely invisible.
Formless as a shadow, its image is likewise!
When there is seeking within phenomena, the mind has already ceased.
If one seeks that mind within these phenomena,
phenomena do not perceive the mind, nor does the mind perceive phenomena.
Regarding such a mind, one seeks the mind within the mind;
when the mind has become thus, all habitual tendencies are fully seen.
All phenomena are likewise so!
There is no one capable of obstructing this Dharma;
whatever thoughts may arise, they cannot cause any hindrance.
All dharmas that are as yet unaccomplished, I shall fully bring them to completion.
That Dharma is like space, eternally abiding without increase or decrease.
Just as in space, that which arises has no inherent existence;
for one who is thus, all phenomena are seen.
Nor does one perform any action within space;
this is what is called "excellent," and all phenomena are likewise so!
The eye does not see the ear, nor does the ear see the eye.
The tongue does not see the nose, nor does the nose see the tongue;
the body does not see the mind, nor does the mind see the body.
Each abides in its own place, and nowhere do they see one another.
Whether heard from others, or known by oneself;
being thus fully capable, one may expound the Dharma-realm for others.
Since the Dharma-realm is such as this, it is entirely equal.
The six decays do not know me, nor do I know the decays.
Thus one fully understands all these matters concerning the dharmas studied;
having trained in this way, one’s wisdom is immeasurable.
To see all the countless billions of Buddhas throughout the ten directions,
and together with their assemblies of disciples, to hear the honored ones preach the Dharma entirely;
and whoever possesses this Dharma, to explain it extensively and universally for the sake of others.
Thereupon, Immeasurable Wisdom became utterly purified;
he heard the excellent exposition of the virtues of the precepts in their fullness;
he understood all discourses and attained complete mastery in their discernment.
They know all things completely, including every thought in the minds of others; then,
by the power of their spiritual feet, they travel through billions of buddha-fields for trillions of kalpas,
as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers.
All that was practiced in previous lives is seen and fully understood;
by means of these very practices, one has attained the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
Consequently, through this, one draws near to the peaceful, unsurpassed enlightenment.
That which the Buddha abides in, all have already attained;
those who have not yet reached the Way should seek its principle through the Way.
Thus, when observing all phenomena, they are all empty and nothing is seen.
He immediately gave rise to a mind of exultation, a joy beyond compare;
not even all the hosts of Māras could move a single hair on his body.
He swiftly attained perfect enlightenment, becoming the unsurpassed and most honored one.
“Devaputra!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the merit of inconceivable skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
What are these four?
First, they attain the wisdom and merit of their previous lives.

Second, regarding those who are without support, those who are cold and frozen, those who suffer, those in pain, and those who are sorrowful—if they see such beings afflicted by these manifold poisons of suffering, they immediately resolve with joyful vigor to rescue them, teaching them all to seek the Buddha-way.

Third, by means of upholding all dharmas, they bind their minds to all beings; they uphold the merit and blessings of their own long-past lives to provide encouragement and assistance, and further uphold the merit and blessings of all past Buddhas to provide encouragement and assistance, causing all to be liberated from sorrow and suffering, released and set free, and finally offering all these merits to those who endure toil, hardship, and calamity.
Fourth, he has never made a resolve that fails to fulfill all vows;
nor has he ever made a resolve that allows sentient beings to fall into outflows or fail to reach the Path;
nor has he ever allowed any being to fail to reach the Path.
Just as my mind desires to reach the Way, the Way also welcomes my mind; likewise, wisdom welcomes the mind, and the mind attains the wisdom of the Way.
Sustaining *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), one increases in merit without causing any disruption to the *dharmadhātu*;
regarding the conceivable dharmas, one never experiences weariness in what is studied.

One does not become weary or satisfied with any meritorious qualities; thus, in performing these merits, one becomes even more insatiable. One loses nothing of the mental factors, nor does the mind lose anything of its meritorious qualities.
They constantly practice generosity with a pure mind, free from expectation;
they constantly uphold the precepts without deficiency or diminution;
and they remain unshakable in the power of patience.
He applies himself to diligence without indolence;
he remains undisturbed in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
and he is not deluded regarding wisdom (*prajñā*).

He constantly makes offerings to all beings without any craving; he repays their kindness with loving-kindness without any anxiety; he contemplates that which is born as being unborn; and he is concerned for the Dharma he preaches, desiring that all may be delivered and liberated.
“O Son of Heaven!
Such is the practice of a bodhisattva!
Those who perceive only small merit do not realize that through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), what is accomplished is infinite and immeasurable.”
In this way, O Devaputra!
Regarding all these dharmas, the bodhisattva attains incalculable wisdom, such that there is nothing among all dharmas that he does not know and nothing that he does not fully understand.
Why is this? O Devaputra!
All dharmas are empty, signless, and wishless.
In this way, emptiness is incalculable; the mind attains the incalculable, and even small meritorious deeds, when performed with *upāyakauśalya*, become infinite and immeasurable.
Why is this? Such a path is immeasurable, and the mind is likewise!

Such practice is immeasurable; the dharmas that are boundless and immeasurable follow those boundless and immeasurable dharmas. Thus, the path-dharmas of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are also boundless and immeasurable.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

By means of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), the bodhisattva excels in all practices; having so excelled, he accords with what all people delight in, and whether they are givers, seekers, or preachers of the Dharma, he delivers and liberates them through the Dharma."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

When a bodhisattva has become thus, having attained the infinite and incalculable dharmas of practice, they will then be fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom."
One harbors no thought of contempt for those who undergo hardships;
one remains without deficiency in the precepts, thereby gaining benefit and growth through them;
one practices patience toward all people, enduring even those who revile or treat one with contempt.
In diligence, they assemble all virtuous qualities;
in meditation, they attain all concentrations;
in wisdom, they are without obstruction.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra, a bodhisattva,
through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), manifests among the disciples and teaches them according to their respective dharmas, yet within himself he harbors no expectations;
he manifests among the pratyekabuddhas and teaches them according to their dharma, yet within himself he harbors no expectations."
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
By means of these four dharmas, a bodhisattva attains inconceivable skillful wisdom (*upāya-kauśalya*).
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"There are two kinds of suffering: that which belongs to oneself and that which belongs to others.
Having extinguished one's own suffering, one is further able to extinguish that of others.
One should concern oneself with all people, causing their minds to comprehend the matters of the Path."
Regarding the Dharma, the mind is likewise; may all be made to understand this single principle.
Using merit for the sake of all people, through diligent practice throughout the three periods of time, may one encourage and assist in all the merits practiced by the Buddhas.
By these merits and blessings, I offer them as a gift to all;
may they swiftly attain the Buddha-wisdom regarding all their heart’s aspirations.
May all who have resolved to seek awakening study the path of the True and Right Way.
The mind does not seek anything further in other paths;
the mind does not hope for a path, for even when looked upon, it cannot be seen.
Such is the characteristic of the path, and the characteristic of the mind is likewise the same!
Dharma and so forth are thus; even in me, there is no self.
Knowing and seeing one's own merit increases pure merit.
There is nothing added to the body; the dharma-realm is inconceivable.
Constantly abiding in the place of the Way, this is what it means to seek the Buddha!
Their minds never harbor thoughts of benefiting themselves through noble status;
their hearts always remain fixed on the Way, practicing with diligence and without slackening.
Practice giving without weariness, always firmly guarding the precepts;
likewise with patience, do not cultivate the faculties of a person.
Practice diligence day by day, and always contemplate the emptiness of the body.
Tranquil in meditative concentration, wisdom can cross over all.
Nurturing all beings, one’s actions are like a lotus flower;
giving and maintaining purity, one expects nothing from others.
Constantly aspiring to seek the Buddha’s wisdom, they fully comprehend all phenomena;
having mastered all dharmas, their wisdom is inconceivable.
They preach the Dharma for the sake of all beings, remaining free from all obstructions.
If one corresponds to this practice, they are indeed a bodhisattva!
Fully understanding emptiness, they give little yet receive immeasurable reward;
they do not conceive of existence or non-existence, and their mind is never indulgent.
Fully knowing all modes of conduct, they deliver others according to their aspirations;
they give as desired and propagate the flourishing transformation through the teaching of the Dharma.
Having given, they feel no regret; in their observance of the precepts, they remain without deficiency.
Patience and diligence, Meditation and wisdom without arrogance;
Generosity and ethical discipline, Patience and diligence;
In meditative concentration and samādhi, Through wisdom and giving, one attains subduing and taming.
Regarding the practices of the śrāvakas, as well as those of the pratyekabuddhas,
he liberates others according to their inclinations, yet does not follow after them internally.
Firmly abiding in this Dharma, the bodhisattva remains without attachment.
“Powerful wisdom is inconceivable; it swiftly attains the subduing of all things.

Furthermore, O Son of Heaven, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva regards all dharmas as having a single flavor, as a single entrance, and as a single teaching, such that their wisdom fully understands and penetrates all doctrines.”
What are these four?

Thus, O Devaputra, a bodhisattva attains the merit of omniscience within the dharma-realm without causing any destruction; they believe that all dharmas are empty, and they do not claim within the dharma-realm that "this is my doing" or "this is not my doing."
Why is this? It is not that "I am the doer," nor is it that "it is not I who am the doer"—both are incorrect. Why is that so?
By destroying all that is unfit for practice, one immediately attains the knowledge that knows all dharmas.
O Son of Heaven!

These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are of one flavor, of one entrance, and of one teaching; such wisdom is fully understood and penetrates the deliberations of all knowledges.
Knowing thus and seeing thus,
whether in the mundane world or on the Path, one turns the wheel of the Dharma with loving-kindness;
and if there are practitioners, they practice accordingly.

If there are those who have shown kindness, one should repay their kindness; if there are those who are unstable, one should establish them—establishing them by means of the Dharma and turning them toward it through great compassion for the Dharma. One does not harbor thoughts of "this person is noble" or "this person is base" regarding various dharmas. Nor does one perceive any fixed habituation within the entry into the Dharma, nor within the practice of the Dharma, nor within manifold dharmas. Knowing the nature of ordinary people's dharmas, one accordingly practices the dharmas of ordinary people; yet regarding these dharmas of ordinary people, one neither elevates nor disparages them. This same principle applies to the destruction of habitual tendencies regarding even a single matter, whereby one then extensively explains all dharmas.
Within the realm of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one does not perceive anything that can be destroyed.
Why is this? Because one has attained the "one forbearance" (*ekakṣānti*) and thus exercises forbearance toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One who endures emptiness without doubt enters into it as one; so too is the entry into all dharmas!

Just as there is an entry into that which is unarisen, O Devaputra, so too does a bodhisattva draw near to the unsurpassed, right, and true path of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, yet he neither conceives of himself as drawing near to the Buddha nor as not drawing near to the Buddha.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the destruction of even a single thing. Why is that?
Nor does one perceive any difference among all persons;
nor does one perceive any difference in the Path;
nor does one perceive any persons at all.
"Furthermore, one does not perceive a path.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"One does not speak of right or wrong within the dharma-realm; One does not cause any destruction within the dharma-realm."
The Dharma-realm is such as all these suchnesses; if one does not contemplate them, their meaning will not be understood.
Having already gained faith that all phenomena are empty, the six sense-decadences will long abide in union with emptiness.
All phenomena being quiescent, one attains mastery; if one place is empty, all others are likewise so.
Regarding phenomena, there is no view and no one who sees; likewise, there is no self that can be apprehended.
If I train until I have attained such realization, I shall truly understand the intent of the Path.
Practice should be tranquil and attain the treasury of emptiness; following cessation, one dwells in the locus of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are inherently still;
therein, in this silent purity, there is nothing that is not permissible.
Knowing all the worldly dharmas of this world, he therein has no doubt and does not turn back;
he does not sever his vows, but aspires for the future and aspires for what is to come; hearing the Dharma, he constantly reflects upon it without indolence or pride.
Throughout incalculable and immeasurable eons, one does not perceive the deeds performed by one's own body;
wandering through the five realms of existence, one does not see the Dharma—only an ordinary person or an Arhat can know it.
Whatever people habitually study and constantly contemplate and speak of—such matters as the dharmas of an Arhat—he neither elevates nor disparages;
it is only through profound stillness and non-attachment that one comes to know them.
He fully knows all categories of phenomena, yet he does nothing to destroy the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*);
his patience is equal to space and without distinction—such is the nature of all phenomena, for they are all like space!
Patience is like space, free from all conceptualization; all phenomena enter into a single wisdom.
Since there is nothing from which they arise, no habits are produced; thus, the path one travels is not difficult.
Thus approaching the immeasurable path, one maintains a mind free from weariness;
whether for oneself or others, when the Dharma is thus realized and nothing sought is found, then one awakens to the Way.
“Devaputra!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva remains heedful regarding profound ethical conduct. What are these four?
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva reflects for himself: "What is called 'precept' (śīla)?
Thus observing his own conduct, he knows that all the good deeds performed by his body, the good words spoken by his mouth, and the good thoughts conceived by his mind are what is called precept.
What are the actions of the body, the words of the mouth, and the thoughts of the mind?
Not committing offenses through bodily acts—namely, not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct—is called "virtuous conduct of the body."
What is wholesome speech?
It is not harsh speech, not divisive speech, not false speech, and not frivolous speech; this is what constitutes wholesome speech.
What is meant by "wholesome mental intention"?
It is being without envy, without ill will, and without wrong views; this is called wholesome mental intention.

Thus, one observes oneself and sees it all clearly. For this reason, one fully attains the conduct of body, speech, and mind as described. If one does not engage in such [unwholesome] deeds, no one would be able to fully describe their merit.
It is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor crimson, yet it is not separate from form;
it cannot be cognized by visual consciousness,
nor can it be cognized through the conceptualization of mental consciousness.
Why is this? Herein, there is no arising and nothing that arises; there is no originating and nothing that originates.

Thus, through this non-arising and the absence of anything arisen, and this non-originating and the absence of anything originated, one attains the virtue of being unable to speak while universally expounding. At that time, the mind dwells in peace without wavering. Thus, there is no meeting with that which cannot be universally expounded; thus, there is no one capable of universal exposition. Furthermore, one does not say of oneself, "I am able to do this," nor does one say, "I am the speaker," nor "I am the practitioner"; even the mind itself is invisible.
Speaking thus of the mind, one likewise cannot perceive any trace of the precepts.
In this way, O Devaputra,
a bodhisattva attains the virtue of the profound precepts.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

A bodhisattva attains the knowledge of the merit of being detached from the perceived body; he knows that within what is perceived there is no arising, and thus neither precepts nor bad precepts, etc., perform any action."

"Furthermore, O Devaputra, when a bodhisattva attains and abides in the profound essentials of the Dharma, he performs such a sacrifice: he practices all the matters of training and all far-reaching conducts, and he practices all the conducts of every vehicle; this is called 'precept' (śīla)."
Acting in this way, one neither deceives oneself nor deceives others; such a person is said to possess the profound precepts.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven, a bodhisattva attains non-violation of the precepts, non-deficiency of the precepts, and non-loss of the precepts."
"How does a bodhisattva not violate the precepts, not diminish the precepts, and not lose the precepts?
O Son of Heaven!
One who is able to protect oneself is thus able to protect the precepts."
"O Son of Heaven!

One who knows for oneself is able to know the precepts; such a person does not treat the precepts with levity, leaves nothing deficient in what they have studied, and does not lose the precepts. It is for this reason that they do not lose the precepts."
One thoroughly knows all phenomena pertaining to others. What is "other"?
And where do I abide?
Nor does he treat others with such stubbornness!
O Son of Heaven!
It is for this reason that he is able to deliver all people.
"O Son of Heaven!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains profound precepts and remains free from negligence."
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“Whatever is practiced by body, speech, and mind, The Dharma is pure and further purified;
That practice surpasses precious jewels— This is the precept for a Bodhisattva!”
These ten are unsurpassed; O wise Bodhisattva who maintains and protects them!
When body, speech, and mind are not deficient, this precept is the most wise.
It is neither created nor produced; within production, there is no production.
Without seed and without abiding place, how could wisdom be attained?
Not meeting and not creating precepts, it cannot be seen by the eye;
nor is it perceived by the ear, nose, or mouth, nor is it cognized by the body or mind.
Not creating the six sense-faculties, that which dwells therein has no location;
this precept is exceedingly pure, yet the precept itself has no place of abiding.
Guarding the precepts without negligence, one harbors no notion of a self regarding the precepts.
Guarding the precepts without the notion of "precepts," one thereby attains profound discipline.
Thus observing the activities of the body, one becomes free from all objects of perception;
not following the locus of conceptual views, one harbors no mental constructions regarding the precepts.
As one enters the profound Dharma according to the Vinaya, all conditioned phenomena are brought to completion;
by extinguishing existence, one is able to provide protection, remaining free from divergent thoughts regarding the precepts.
Where there is a self, there is a precept; where there is no self, there is also no precept.
This is called fear; knowing me, one possesses the precepts.
The precept of emptiness and stillness is without thought; the precept of tranquility is without attachment.
The precept of emptiness and stillness is without time; the tranquil precept is without conceptualization.
Not failing in the unsurpassed precepts, being without arrogance regarding the precepts,
and having no notion of a self in the precepts— this is the profound precept.
Being exceedingly courageous and resolute in the precepts, one does not commit what is unwholesome.
One who possesses the precepts yet performs manifold practices finds all dharmas unattainable.
To have the notion of "precepts" is delusion; to speak of "observing the precepts" while having no precepts is likewise so.
This is the destruction of the fruit of the precepts, and one shall not escape the five realms of existence.
Distant from all views, one perceives nothing as "mine";
In the precepts, too, there is nothing perceived, and thus one does not fear the five realms of existence.
Seeing that which is non-seeing as seeing, one does not increase unwholesome conduct.
"Be free from illness regarding me, and you shall fully perceive the practice of the precepts.
The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Foot-Powers, Scroll One.
The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Foot-Powers, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thereupon, the Moon Deva addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! This is truly marvelous.
The profound subtlety of the Tathāgata is indeed such as this!”
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, is unsurpassed, truly correct, and most marvelous.

The practices performed by a bodhisattva are such that they are called "the practice of seeing all dharmas with one's own eyes. They do not give rise to conduct that seeks self-pleasure or benefits the body at the expense of the Way; rather, from long ago, they have severed and abandoned the perception of a body. Having practiced for incalculable eons, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor do they decline, but bring the Way to ultimate completion and fulfill the Buddha-dharmas. How many such practices are there?
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the profound Dharma, do they not realize it under hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas?
The Buddha said to the devaputra:
“Bodhisattvas have four qualities by which they attain the practice of the profound Dharma, yet do not realize it in the presence of hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas.
What are these four?
It is thus, O Devaputra!”
The Bodhisattva firmly abides in the essential dharmas and maintains all-encompassing wisdom; having left the household life, he roars like a lion, attaining vigor that is never weak.
For the sake of all beings, he relinquishes all possessions; firmly abiding in generosity, he thereby achieves the work of great compassion.
As the Buddha has taught and as he has questioned, they have answered all accordingly, having attained skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Having already perfected all merits, they further accomplish other virtues.
"O Son of Heaven!
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva practices the profound Dharma and does not seek realization under hundreds of thousands of millions of countless Buddhas.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke these verses:
Firmly abiding in what is to be done, their wisdom is likewise so!
The wisdom cultivated in previous lives they never abandon.
Because of their omniscience, they have no anxiety regarding what they undertake.
All forms and appearances, he fully understands them all.
His conduct is always characterized by diligence; he never succumbs to negligence.
His mind is never weary or indolent; his practice is likewise so!
Whatever actions they perform, they do so out of concern for all;
thus, toward sentient beings, they always maintain an impartial mind.
Constantly giving rise to the intention of great compassion, they feel anxiety and concern for all people.
Compassionately pitying all who suffer toil and hardship, I desire to bring them all peace and security.
May I swiftly attain Buddhahood and sever all suffering and affliction;
may I obtain all manner of rare treasures, the store of which shall never be exhausted.
Constantly employing the wisdom of skillful means, he teaches various expedients;
He exerts diligent effort to cultivate merit, practicing these without weariness or satiety.
His undertakings reach ultimate fulfillment, and his conduct is always in accordance with what is appropriate.
Establishing them in the sequence of the Path, one does not dwell on thoughts of home or dwelling;
those who possess such a Dharma all maintain it with firm resolve;
the Bodhisattva who practices this fully understands all modes of conduct.
"In this most profound Dharma, all practices are fully perfected;
toward hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, one never tires in what is done.
At that time, the Devaputra Candra asked the Buddha:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the practice of profound depth?
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"A bodhisattva does not have expectations regarding the dharmas of ordinary people, nor do they seek anything within the dharmas of the Buddhas; nor do they harbor doubts regarding the dharmas of ordinary people. To them, the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of ordinary people are no different."
One does not seek anything within the dharmas of ordinary persons, nor is there anything gained or lost regarding the dharmas of the Buddha;
one is no different from ordinary persons, and no different from the dharmas of the Buddha.
Nor does he form such a thought:
he does not say that the dharmas of ordinary persons are inferior, nor that the Buddha-dharmas are superior;
he neither abandons the dharmas of ordinary persons, nor does he abandon the Buddha-dharmas.
Thus, birth after birth and birth again—this is called the nature of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
These two dharmas—the Buddha-dharma and the ordinary-person dharma—are empty, quiescent, and settled; thus they are known as being without location.
Nor does one seek anything within the dharmas of ordinary persons, nor does one seek anything within the dharmas of the Buddhas;
there is nothing to be found within the sphere of the dharmas of ordinary persons, nor is there anything to be found within the sphere of the dharmas of the Buddhas.
Regarding these two, one neither perceives an ordinary person nor perceives a non-ordinary person.
To know thus is to be in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*).
That which is seen by the eye—all that is seen—is empty, signless, and also wishless.
Such is the suchness of wisdom, and such is the suchness of what is seen by the eye; this wisdom is the Buddha-dharma, yet it neither exists nor does not exist in the Buddha.
One does not think of it as having ease or suffering, nor does one think of it as beautiful or ugly; all these are empty.
It is also like emptiness within emptiness; one does not perceive emptiness within emptiness, nor does one know it, nor seek it. Why is this?
This is because they have already become habituated to aging and arising.
"In this way, O Devaputra!
Dharmas abide in dharmas; this is called the abiding of dharmas, the cessation of dharmas, and the tranquility of dharmas. In this, one neither perceives oneself nor perceives anything at all."
Furthermore, they do not know themselves, nor is there anything known.

Why is this? Whether it be an ordinary person, a disciple, a pratyekabuddha, a samyaksambuddha, one who has received the prediction [of enlightenment], or one of profound practice—O Devaputra! [It is thus.]
A bodhisattva does not [perceive] emptiness in phenomena, nor emptiness in the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? O Devaputra, it is because: [as follows].
Regarding the Dharma, it is the sound of the Dharma; that which is a good sound is a good sound, yet it cannot be apprehended therein.
Since it is thus unapprehendable, therein it is without self (*anātman*);
since it is thus without self, one does not speak of abiding or non-abiding as one departs.
"O Son of Heaven!
All dharmas are thus incalculable, and the Buddha-dharma is no different from them.
O Son of Heaven!"
The analogy is as follows: one should view all phenomena and the Buddha-dharma in this way, constantly mindful and practicing accordingly.

Furthermore, being mindful of such practice, one gives rise to non-conceptual mindfulness and acts with non-conceptual mindfulness; regarding the Buddha-dharma, one has no further deliberation. One who acts thus is said to be in accord with contemplation and its arising.
One no longer produces such [discursive] knowledge, nor does one add anything to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); it neither exists nor does it not exist.
Furthermore, in practicing the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), one is unable to increase or decrease anything regarding phenomena. Why is this?
Whether there are phenomena characterized by craving or phenomena devoid of craving, one clearly perceives what constitutes craving and what constitutes the absence of craving.
Having already understood this, one no longer follows after it.
Therefore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva who has attained the practice of profound depth ultimately does not perceive any dharma; nor do they ever view, see, or contemplate the Buddha-dharma in such a manner, for they do not engage in such viewing by way of non-perception.
"O Devaputra!
Regarding this teaching, neither Māra nor the gods of Māra can destroy the assembly of bodhisattvas.
O Devaputra!"
"The Buddha has spoken thus!
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The deeds performed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are most extraordinary; they fully comprehend these various matters of wisdom and thus understand birth and death as they truly are. They seek the Way in this manner without weariness or indolence. How could such arising and ceasing, ascending and descending, ever come to an end?
The Buddha said,
"Devaputra! It is like an illusion, like a magical transformation."
Whether coming or going, or sitting;
whether seeking or speaking—all these, too, are non-existent.
O Devaputra!
Just as an illusion, one should know that all phenomena are exactly like this!
All things that arise and cease—whether in the past, the future, or the present—their kalpas are also like this!
"The Bodhisattva does not even think of arising, nor does he think of the practices performed in previous lives.
The Devaputra asked again:
"How is this so, World-Honored One?"

If a bodhisattva does not conceive of a place of arising or birth, why was the Buddha able to come up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, go to his mother’s dwelling, and remain there for the entire three-month summer retreat?
“Does the World-Honored One not arise from Māyā?
The Buddha replied to the devaputra, saying:

“That which the Tathāgata gives birth to does not employ the dharmas of birth and death; he abides in the abiding of suchness (*tathatā*). Suchness neither comes nor goes; the birth of a Buddha is thus.”
The Buddha spoke again:
"Son of Heaven!
The Buddha is born from the Prajñāpāramitā; all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? O Devaputra,
the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are not born from Māyā.
One should train in the Prajñāpāramitā in this way; the Prajñāpāramitā is the body of the Mother of Buddhas, for all thirty-two marks of a Great Man are learned from the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Devaputra Candra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have reflected deeply upon the Prajñāpāramitā as being without arising and without cessation;
why then does the World-Honored One say, ‘The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas’?”

The Buddha replied: "As the Son of Heaven has said, a bodhisattva should train in what is to be trained by a bodhisattva. Upon attaining the *prajñāpāramitā*, he shall obtain the thirty-two marks of a great man that constitute the Buddha-body; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the samādhis of great kindness and great compassion. He shall walk alone with sovereign stride, and the Buddha-wisdom that knows the minds of others shall all come to take refuge in him. None of these, however, are born from Māyā."
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
You should know that the Buddha’s wisdom arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
There are countless and incalculable matters concerning this wisdom; now I have briefly cited these examples, and all such cases are exactly like this.
The devaputra asked again:
"Are the dharmas of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, fully endowed with suchness? Is the suchness of the Tathāgata attained in accordance with suchness?
[The Buddha replied: "It is so, devaputra!"

View all perceived phenomena in this manner: the Buddha is born from the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the *prajñāpāramitā* is not born from him; he has no conceptual root regarding phenomena, nor does he give rise to roots, nor does he engage in contention or elimination.
“How is it, World-Honored One, that the Prajñāpāramitā is produced?
He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
"According to the Dharma, O Devaputra, that which is the Tathāgata’s suchness (tathatā) does not arise, does not originate, and does not cease within the dharmas as they are performed.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!"

Non-arising, non-origination, and non-extinction—such as this, such as this is what constitutes wisdom. This wisdom arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*, and is thus called "the Tathāgata born from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Such arising is non-arising again, non-origination, and non-extinction.
In this way, O Devaputra!
By being unborn, unarisen, and unceasing, the bodhisattva trains swiftly and draws near to the prajñāpāramitā.
Devaputra!
"The wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible, and furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā itself is inexhaustible.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should one contemplate this wisdom?
How should one know that this Prajñāpāramitā is the inexhaustible knowledge?
He spoke again:
“Devaputra! There is no wisdom that exists through the conceptualization of wisdom.
It is thus, Devaputra!”
Regarding wisdom, there is that which possesses conceptualization and possesses knowledge; this is not true wisdom, nor is it inexhaustible wisdom.
Why is this so? O Devaputra!
The mind knows there is effort, yet it can never fully grasp that which is inexhaustible; to act in such a manner would not constitute wisdom.
O Devaputra!
Wisdom is non-conceptual wisdom; if wisdom were subject to exhaustion, it would not be wisdom.
The devaputra asked again:
“How is it, World-Honored One?
Regarding that which is inexhaustible, from what does one inquire and from what does one know?”
He replied: "O Devaputra!
This is inexhaustible; it is not sought through indulgence, but through equanimity."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
To what category does this 'non-laxity' belong?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!

One does not abandon unwholesome actions within the three realms, nor does one depart from them; yet, having already departed from the unwholesome actions within the three realms, one further abandons all unwholesome conduct of the three realms. It is thus, O Devaputra!"
"Each should act according to what is required without indulgence. "What is its retribution?
"Its retribution is neither arising nor ceasing within the three realms."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
Is there any disciple who, having traveled from this place, passes through the three realms to preach the Dharma for the sake of others?"
The Buddha said: "Devaputra!
One may be able to teach the Dharma for disciples within the realm of desire, yet one cannot bring benefit to the realm of desire itself."
To preach the Dharma for disciples within the realm of form and the formless realm is of no benefit at all.

While one may travel through the three realms by means of samādhi and preach the Dharma, such a person cannot fully comprehend what the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught; nor do they see that by the power of samādhi, one can travel through the desire realm and preach while remaining without form.
"Son of Heaven!

Although you roam within the realm of desire, you are still unable to achieve liberation. Even if you roam through the realm of form and the formless realm by the power of samādhi, that which is taught in the formless realm will be of no benefit; you will be entirely unable to achieve liberation within the realms of form and the formless. Though you roam through the three realms, you can only liberate yourself and cannot benefit others."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

Although he knows the three realms, he does not crave them; he sits guarding the dharma of emptiness, nor does he practice in the realm of desire, nor can he abide in the realm of form, nor again can he abide in the formless realm.
Thus, one cannot abide within the triple world, yet neither is one born within the triple world nor is one born from it; even where one goes, that place is unknown.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
These individuals cast off their bodies in this place, yet no one can know it;
neither is their departure seen, nor is their return seen. Why is this?
"O Son of Heaven! All phenomena do not encounter one another within the three realms.
For example, space is unborn, invisible, and has no creator; it does not again assemble with the past."
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
All phenomena within the triple world are exactly like this!
When this Dharma was spoken, among the assembly of devas, seventy-two thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and removed from defilement regarding all phenomena.
Sixteen thousand devaputras, who had already performed meritorious deeds in previous lives, now heard this Dharma being preached and all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the entire assembly, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, each saw for themselves flowers never seen before upon their laps; they all scattered them over the Buddha.
Instantly, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, these flowers filled the entirety of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly marvelous, World-Honored One!
These flowers scattered by these sons of noble family are such as I have never seen before."
At that time, the Devaputra Candra said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!
The Blessed One is likewise one who has never been seen before; the flower is also like this!"
Why is this? Kauśika!
This mind that perceives the World-Honored One while holding onto it is itself extinguished and cannot be perceived.
"Thus it is, Kauśika!
Whatever things can be seen, none of them have ever been seen before.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked the devaputra:
“How do you, O virtuous one, perceive the Buddha?
The devaputra replied,
“Just as the World-Honored One perceives me, so too do I perceive the World-Honored One!”
Śakra Devānām Indra asked again:
"How does one see? He replied:
“Kauśika! The Tathāgata is suchness;
form is suchness; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suchness. It is by seeing the Tathāgata in this way that I see him.
Kauśika!”
I do not perceive the Tathāgata by means of form;
nor do I perceive the Tathāgata by means of sensation,
perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Form is by its very nature neither arising nor ceasing; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise!
This is the characteristic of the phenomena of the five aggregates; these characteristics and non-characteristics are both like universal illumination.
Kauśika! Thus the Tathāgata is invisible. Kauśika!
"Furthermore, those who wish to see the Tathāgata should see me as they would see the Buddha; my seeing of the Buddha is likewise.
He asked again, "Devaputra!"
"How is it that you see the Buddha?
The devaputra replied, "The Buddha is here now; you may ask the Buddha yourself."
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, World-Honored One?
Does the Tathāgata see the Moon Deity?”
The Buddha said:
"One does not see by means of form, nor does one see by means of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does one see by means of the past, nor does one see by means of the future, nor does one see by means of the present."
Nor is it seen as an ordinary person, nor is it seen as the liberation of an ordinary person;
nor is it seen in terms of those in training (*śaikṣa*), nor is it seen in terms of the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
nor is it seen as an Arhat, nor is it seen in terms of the dharmas of an Arhat.
Nor does one see it in the dharma of the disciples, nor does one see it in the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, nor does one see it in the stage of the Buddhas.
Such is what is seen, Kauśika!
In this way one sees the Buddha;
seeing the Buddha in this way is to see nothing at all. This "seeing nothing" is called equal seeing (*samyag-darśana*); such a manifestation is called the manifestation of all things.
Kauśika, when one contemplates with such discerning observation,
this is called the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is without any deficiency or diminution within the dharma-realm.
Kauśika! What do you think, Kauśika?
When the Tathāgata sees in this way and contemplates in this way, what is it that he sees?
He replied:
"World-Honored One, this is called seeing the Buddha."
“The Tathāgata is called ‘attainment,’ yet it is not so with respect to form; regarding this, there is no one who can calculate or conceive of an attainment of the Tathāgata.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is this how one sees the Buddha?
He replied, "It is so."

Kauśika! When a bodhisattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), they abide equally within all dharma-realms; yet, they do not perceive dharmas as being separate from these dharmas.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Has this Moon God attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena?
The Buddha replied to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Take this matter and ask the Devaputra Candra yourself; he shall provide you with an explanation.
Thereupon, Śakra-devānām-indra asked the Devaputra Candra:
"O Benevolent One!"
"Have you now attained this patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena?
The Devaputra Candra replied, "Kauśika!"
"Is it possible for that which is unarisen to arise?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "No."
The devaputra spoke again:
"Kauśika! If there is that which is unarisen and does not come into being, why do you ask further?"
"Have you attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena?
The devaputra spoke again: "Kauśika!
"The Dharma-realm is without anything produced; its analogy is precisely like this. Therefore, the Dharma-realm neither arises nor ceases, and it is entirely unknowable.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra had this thought:
"As the Devaputra Candra has spoken, has he already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas?"
"Is it for the sake of drawing near to Buddhahood?
Or is it for the sake of attaining *samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that time, the Devaputra Candra, knowing what Śakra Devānām Indra was thinking in his mind, spoke to Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“Kauśika! For one who possesses the patience of non-attainment, attaining the seat of *samyaksambodhi* is not difficult;
for one who does not possess this patience, the seat of *samyaksambodhi* is very far away.”
Śakra Devānām Indra spoke again:
"Devaputra, why do you speak thus?"
The devaputra replied: "Kauśika!
Only those who have attained patience can speak thus; those who have not attained this cannot draw near to the seat of the Samyaksaṃbuddha-Avayaṃbuddha."
"Because one has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena, one can speak of that which is non-arisen as being like that which does not arise; such is the Path.
Śakra Devānām-indra again asked the devaputra:
"From where is the Path to be sought?"
The devaputra replied: "Kauśika!
The Way is without self within the triple world; one should seek the Way in this manner."
Śakra Devānām Indra asked again:
"In the three realms there is no self; how, then, can one seek it?
The devaputra replied:
"That which accords with the Dharma does not arise; that which does not arise does not arise again. One should seek the Way in this manner.
Having sought in this way, such seeking is non-seeking; for one who seeks in this way, there is nothing that arises."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly marvelous,
World-Honored One!"
“The profound teaching spoken by the Moon Devaputra is truly such!
From where did he pass away to come and be born here, and having passed away from this place, where will he be reborn?
At that time, the Moon Devaputra spoke to Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"Kauśika! Suppose a magician creates a man or a woman by means of illusion; from where did they pass away to be born here, and having passed away from this place, where will they be reborn?"
Śakra Devānām Indra replied again to the devaputra:
"Illusions and transformations have neither arising nor ceasing; they cannot be seen and cannot be known; they are non-existent."
The devaputra said to Kauśika:
"As you have spoken regarding illusion and transformation, they arise from non-union and, upon ceasing, likewise return to the state of non-union."
"Such an illusion is neither utilized nor avoided by those who possess wisdom.
Śakra Devānām Indra said, "It is so."
"O Devaputra!
It is as you have said.
The Devaputra replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Kauśika! Just as you have asked, so too is my answer.
As for you, all phenomena are like illusions; it was with this thought that you wished to hold onto this matter and question the Buddha."
"From where did this devaputra pass away to come and be born here, and where will he pass away from here to be reborn?
The devaputra said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"What do you think, Kauśika?"
"Suppose there were a transformation created by a Tathāgata; would that which was transformed, or its suchness, be visible or knowable as going, coming, ascending, or descending?
Śakra Devānām-indra replied:
"O Devaputra!"
"In this way, it cannot be perceived.
The devaputra spoke again:
"Can this transformation perform any action?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"One is able to perform [such deeds].
The devaputra spoke again:
"So it is, Kauśika! The transformation of all dharmas is just like this, whether they go, come, ascend, or descend."
"Kauśika, when one contemplates in this way,
there is nothing that can be produced therein.
What do you think, Kauśika?"
One does not see them here; it is the same for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena!
Could such a person created by transformation (nirmāṇa-puruṣa) possibly see, hear, or know such things?
Śakra Devānām-indra said:
"O Son of Heaven!
It cannot be seen, heard, or known."
The devaputra said: “So it is, Kauśika!”
In this way, regarding all such categories, one knows that all phenomena are likewise!
Whether seen, heard, or mentally conceived as phenomena, they neither stain nor defile;
nor does one dwell therein.
Neither approaching nor departing,
regarding what is seen, heard, or remembered— such words and such dharmas are spoken for all, and that which is spoken for the assembly is without any difference.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Moon God has spoken of that which has no location, is unarisen, does not originate, and does not cease.”
This devaputra is not seen to be on the level of the disciples, nor is he seen to be on the level of the bodhisattvas.
How then can a bodhisattva recollect the events of birth and death throughout incalculable kalpas? Why is it that the manner in which they nurture sentient beings cannot be known at all?
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!

Any bodhisattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) does not conceive of birth, does not conceive of arising, and does not conceive of cessation.”
If you wish to behold such bodhisattvas, you should regard them as one observes an arhat who has entered parinirvāṇa for a hundred years—incapable of being apprehended. Why is this so?
Because they possess neither the notion of another nor the notion of a self.
Furthermore, there is no perception of others, nor is there a perception of self; it is likewise, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva who practices with diligence, delighting in the exertion of asceticism, does not conceive thoughts of arising, nor does he conceive thoughts of ceasing.
Furthermore, there is no perception of others, nor is there a perception of self; the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is fundamentally nirvāṇa.
Thus, Kauśika, all things are neither bound nor liberated.

Because they do not fully comprehend these dharmas, for this reason the bodhisattva acts for their liberation and provides them with instruction; it is through such reflection that he gives rise to great compassion.
This bodhisattva does not grow weary; throughout incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, they do not slacken.

For example, Kauśika, suppose there were a person fallen into a fire pit, and a man of great compassion—disregarding his own body and not sparing his own life—were to abandon the five desires and all pleasures, enter the fire pit, take that person in his arms and pull them out, emerging himself as well as delivering that person.
"What do you think, Kauśika?
Is what this person does difficult?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“World-Honored One!
What this person has done is most difficult, most difficult!
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Kauśika! What is there that is difficult about this?"

The deeds performed by a bodhisattva are even more difficult than this: having liberated themselves from all desires, they resolve to maintain various articles of offering, and with whatever they possess, they protect and bestow them upon all beings.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

There are those who surpass even this, for by the virtue of this radiance they illuminate and reveal all things; in this way, they all transcend the level of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as the bodhisattva mahāsattvas themselves attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
From where did such a person as you pass away to be reborn here?
Listen, Kauśika!"
In this division of the eastern direction, passing from this buddha-field across ninety-two hundred thousand nayutas of buddha-fields, there is a land named Ratnasañcaya (in the language of Jin:
*Zhēnbǎo Shěndì Àozàng*, meaning "Precious and Thoroughly Verified Profound Treasury").

In that world, trees are made of various jewels, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits being of infinite colors. The places for walking meditation are fashioned from countless jewels, and everything within that land is adorned with various jewels without any empty space; the ground is entirely of deep blue lapis lazuli, interspersed with countless other jewels.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
There is a world named Ratanārciḥ— translated into Chinese as 'Accumulation of Precious Jewels'."
In this world, Kauśika!
there is a Buddha named Ratnavicitraketudhvajarāja (in the language of Jin:
*Zhenbao haochang chushang ju*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently dwelling and preaching the Dharma.
In that Buddha-land there are no women, nor is the word "woman" even heard;
furthermore, there are no followers of the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, for the entire buddha-field is filled solely with bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

From this field of precious jewels, there emerged a superior assembly of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. As each of those World-Honored Ones preached the Dharma, seventy-two koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattikadharmakṣānti)."

Once the Bodhisattva has attained this patience, he reflects that all things—whether noble reputation, abundant treasures, celestial realms, or worldly greatness—are entirely severed; for this reason, all Buddha-fields tremble for him.

Immediately, within this trichiliocosm, countless varieties of precious jewels, lotuses, and diverse flowers—of exceedingly brilliant and beautiful colors—filled the space and were scattered over the Buddha; they all transformed above the Buddha into flower canopies.

Having completely covered the Buddha-fields, these bodhisattvas then leaped into the air and flew to the presence of Buddhas in other directions to make offerings and pay homage; they desired to circumambulate them and inquire after their well-being, and they desired to hear the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva who has attained the patience toward dharmas does not delight in dwelling in a single place, but is able to travel everywhere to all buddha-fields;
a bodhisattva who has not attained the patience toward dharmas cannot reach other regions."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Twelve kalpas have passed since that Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared. In the place where that Buddha resides, he constantly preaches the Dharma three times each night.
Having preached the Dharma, seventy-two koṭis of bodhisattvas have attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
Thus it is, Kauśika!

A bodhisattva who has not attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) cannot go to other buddha-fields; only one who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas can go to other buddha-fields. Such a bodhisattva passes away from here and is born in other buddha-fields.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
You should regard it by this analogy; all the bodhisattvas in incalculable billions of buddha-fields are exactly like this! "Kauśika!"

In that world-system of Accumulated Precious Jewels, there is nothing whatsoever that involves entering the three evil realms; there is neither the cognition of suffering nor the cognition of pleasure;
there is neither questioning nor teaching;
and there is neither exertion or toil nor food or drink.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas take the joy of the Dharma as their food and drink; in that land, even the names of arhats and pratyekabuddhas do not exist.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

Within the land of Ratnasaṃcaya, there is a World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnavyūhottarasaṃcayagiri. This Moon Deva-son has passed away from that Buddha-field and been reborn here in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; he has come because he wishes to see the Buddha, to pay homage to me, circumambulate me, and inquire after my well-being, having come for the purpose of asking a question.

By means of these questions, thousands of people gathered there gained extensive knowledge, and furthermore, other bodhisattvas present were all brought to full completion in their realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Kauśika! This Moon Deva-son has come specifically to see the Buddha, desiring to protect all dharmas and to uphold the Dharma.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the final dharma is about to perish, he shall attain the Way here and be born among humans. He will uphold these most profound and profound dharmas as they were spoken, illuminating them extensively and universally instructing a full hundred thousand people; therein, through the patience regarding non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), they shall all joyfully desire to study for a long time."

When the Dharma is about to perish at the end of time, he will pass away there and be reborn in the fourth Tuṣita Heaven. There, he will join the assembly of Maitreya Bodhisattva and discourse upon the matters of the path of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras who had never previously aroused the aspiration for enlightenment will, upon hearing this teaching, all resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When Maitreya descends and attains perfect enlightenment, this bodhisattva will serve Maitreya Buddha for ten thousand years. While remaining at home, he will constantly make offerings to Maitreya and the assembly of monks; subsequently, together with four thousand people, he will leave his household life out of faith to practice the Way and become a śramaṇa.
Having become a śramaṇa, he shall constantly uphold the Dharma for as long as his life lasts under Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
and after Maitreya has entered parinirvāṇa, he shall continue to uphold the Dharma for as long as the Dharma remains.
Thus, among the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, with four Buddhas yet to appear, you shall all make offerings to and serve that many Buddhas.

You shall cultivate the pure conduct of *brahmacarya* according to the sūtras spoken by those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Finally, after the passing of kalpas equal to seven *gaṅgā* rivers of sands, you shall become Buddhas in this world, named Candraprabha (Moonlight) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with all your vows fulfilled.
Thereupon, the devaputra Candraketu spoke to that devaputra, saying:
"Excellent!
You have now been granted a prophecy by the Buddha; you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"What kind of kindness did you originally have?
What kind of offerings did you make?
What kind of acts of love, respect, joy, delight, and joyful giving did you perform for the Buddha, such that the Tathāgata has granted you this prediction alone?"
At that time, the Devaputra Candra said to the Devaputra Candraketu:
"The Tathāgata does not deliver a verdict for others out of favoritism;
nor does he deliver a verdict for others because of fear."
Nor did he say that this person may be given [the prediction] or that one may not.
A bodhisattva simply trains in the bodhisattva-dharma, and the World-Honored One then bestows upon them the prediction of certainty.
Why do you ask such a question?
"What kindness have I shown to the Buddha that causes him to treat me with such respect, such affection, such mindfulness, such joy, and such gifts?"
The Devaputra Candraketu asked the Devaputra Candra,
"From where should this joy be seen?
