The Devaputra Candra replied to the Devaputra Candraketu:
"Joy is sought from within the mind.
The Devaputra Candranakṣatra spoke again:
"If the mind does not conceive of the mind, who is it that leaps for joy?"
He replied:
"This exultation is ungraspable and cannot be attained; it is the supreme exultation.
Because it cannot be attained, it is the pinnacle of all exultations."
The Moon Deva-putra said to the Moon Star Deva-putra:

"To leap forth in this manner—wherein there is nothing improper in this leaping forth—is not to leap for the sake of heedlessness; rather, it is to leap within this state of leaping, never again giving rise to thoughts of decline or regression."
Thus it is, Moon Star Devaputra!
You should seek within this Dharma; for this reason, you attain exultation.
Act with heedfulness regarding what is to be done in the Dharma; therein seek, therein do not seek, and yet do not depart from seeking.
Why is this? Because one does not seek within the dharma-realm,
nor does one seek that which is sought.
"So it is, Devaputra Candraketu!
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Dàoshénzú Wújí Biànhuà Jīng* (Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Power of the Way), Fascicle Two.
The Buddha Spoke the Scripture on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footing, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fāqīn of Parthia during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Moon Star addressed the Devaputra Moon, saying: "Such is the training of a Bodhisattva; it is called..."
"One who trains as a bodhisattva.
He asked again:
"What is this training of a bodhisattva?"
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!

A bodhisattva trains as a bodhisattva by being without body and without bodily action, without speech and without verbal action, and without mind and without mental action; this is the training of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva has nothing to learn regarding the body, nor anything to acquire; there is nothing to lose, nor anything to perish. It is in this way, O Devaputra, that a Bodhisattva trains.
He spoke again:
"Son of Heaven!
Is one who trains in this manner granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Tathāgata?"
The Devaputra Candra said to the Devaputra Candraketu:
"No. The World-Honored One does not grant a definitive prediction to one who trains in such a manner."

Why is this? It is because one does not dwell on this training, does not dwell on that which is spoken, does not dwell on a self, does not dwell on that which is sought, and does not dwell on the thought "I have something to learn"—this is called training.
The classification of speech does not accord with worldly convention. If anyone says, "I study in this way," it is neither true nor a correct teaching;
they do not think, "There is a self," nor do they say, "This is the truth," nor do they say, "I am a bodhisattva who studies."
He asked again:
"If there are certain matters, O Devaputra,
by which one may dwell in the state of verified certainty?"
He replied:

“Regarding one’s vow, it is always held aloft—neither sinking nor wavering in the interim—and the vow is ever present in the mind without ever ceasing or slackening. Although this is so, one does not treat this as a dharma; rather, for this to be the supreme dharma, one must thoroughly and precisely awaken to and know this very dharma. This is called ‘abiding,’ and it is abiding in thorough precision.”
He asked again:
"Celestial Son!
By upholding what dharma do you receive the Tathāgata’s prediction of enlightenment?"

He replied, “I have not abandoned anything regarding the dharmas of ordinary people, nor have I attained anything regarding the dharmas of the Buddha; for this reason, the Tathāgata has bestowed upon me this prediction.”
"O Son of Heaven!
Thus, in this Dharma there is nothing to be relinquished, and in this Dharma there is nothing to be attained; for this reason, I have been granted the prediction of enlightenment by the Tathāgata.
He asked again:
"In this way, all ordinary persons are granted the prediction [of enlightenment]. Why is this?
Because 'suchness' does not abandon ordinary persons, nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary persons; furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, nothing is to be attained."
He spoke again:
"Son of Heaven!
By what causes and conditions does one become subject to the dharmas of ordinary persons?"
He spoke again:
"Is phenomena empty, and is the dharma-realm also empty?
He spoke again:
“Devaputra! For what reason is the suchness of the Buddha-dharma the same as the suchness of the Koṭi Buddhas?
He replied:
“Son of Heaven!
Is it possible to relinquish anything within the realm of space or the realm of phenomena?
He replied:
“Devaputra! Is there anything to be attained regarding the Tathāgata Kuli Buddha?
He replied:
"Not for long,
O devaputra! Indeed,
not for long, O devaputra!"
Explaining in sequence: regarding the dharmas of ordinary persons, there is nothing to be relinquished;
regarding the dharmas of the Buddha, there is nothing to be attained.
To act in this manner is what constitutes receiving the prediction of enlightenment from the Tathāgata.
He spoke again:
"How is it that one attains certainty regarding the realm of space, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), suchness (tathatā), and the *koṭi* of Buddhas?
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
It is not so. He asked again:
"What do you think, Devaputra?

If one does not attain certainty regarding the realm of space, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), suchness (tathatā), and the *koṭī* of Buddhas, from what else could one possibly obtain certainty regarding other Buddhas?"
He replied:
"The Tathāgata is as one who has received the prediction; the realm of emptiness and the dharma-realm are the Tathāgata Koṭī Buddha.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!"
The Dharma is such as this; the Dharma is such as this. When one is thus granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa), this is called receiving the prediction.
Having received the prediction, one does not depart from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor does one depart from the state of an avaivartika Buddha.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Candraketu came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Devaputra Candra has attained profound wisdom; that which he has spoken is indeed such as this?"
The Buddha said:
"It is thus, O Devaputra, that a bodhisattva,
for the sake of attaining patience, either seeks or dispatches this teaching of the Dharma."

Regarding all realms of phenomena (dharmadhātu), whether one speaks or there is something spoken, one cannot have any perception of the realm of phenomena, nor can one utter anything, nor can one transmit anything.
Why is this? Within the dharma-realm there is nothing to be spoken and nothing to be explained;
such is the dharma-realm, and such is the realm of persons.
In this way, the realm of beings is the locus of the Buddha’s power; in this way, all dharmas are likewise the locus of the Buddha’s power!
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

When a bodhisattva abides in accordance with the Dharma in this manner, thus abiding he no longer places faith in other matters, nor does he follow after other matters. For one who is thus, on what basis would there be anything further for the Buddha to explain?
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was preaching the Dharma to the assembly of devaputras in the Indrānila Palace of Śakra Devānām Indra.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat and began to wander about, thinking to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is here; Jambudvīpa has become empty for him."

In Jambudvīpa, there are countless people who are hungry and empty, desiring to cultivate merit; yet because they do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, their practice of wholesome deeds diminishes.

Thereupon, having formed this thought, Mahāmaudgalyāyana exercised his divine eye to survey Jambudvīpa. He then saw the Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—eating in the palace of Piṅgala, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana again saw himself seated to the left of the Buddha; he saw his own body and attire sitting beside the Buddha without any change or diminution, and he further reflected:
"Could it be that the World-Honored One has returned to Jambudvīpa?"

He looked again toward the foot of the Pāṭali tree and saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of devas as he preached the Dharma. He saw Śāriputra seated to the Buddha’s right, and saw himself, Maudgalyāyana, together with the bhikṣus, seated to the Buddha’s left, also in the company of a great assembly of bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw what was most marvelous and extraordinary:

"The deeds performed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are inconceivable. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such majestic power and such great capability that while they preach the Dharma in Jambudvīpa as before without interruption, they simultaneously preach the Dharma for the sake of the devas upon the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was again greatly astonished and marveled; he looked once more with keen attention.
He saw the Buddha at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude as he preached the Dharma for them.

Furthermore, he saw himself present within the assembly in his own likeness; Śāriputra, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇa, Subhūti, the venerable Revata, and the son of Kapphiṇa—all the great disciples—were likewise seen, as if they were in Śrāvastī, as if in Rājagṛha, or as if in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana again contemplated Jambudvīpa; he saw the great kingdom of Kapilavastu and the Nyagrodha tree, and he saw the Buddha emerge from the Nyagrodha Garden and enter the great kingdom of Kapilavastu to wander for alms.

Again he saw a bhikṣu whose appearance was like that of Maudgalyāyana; thereupon he further saw the Buddha in the great kingdom of Vaiśālī together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, having gone to the house of the youth Vimalacandra for a meal.

Maudgalyāyana again saw his own physical form and appearance together with a great assembly of bhikṣus; there, Mahā-Maudgalyāyana saw the Buddha returning from his alms-round in the great kingdom of Vārāṇasī, and he saw his own physical form and appearance also among them.

He further reflected and surveyed Jambudvīpa everywhere; in every location he saw Buddhas—whether beneath trees or among rocky crags—and the entire surface of Jambudvīpa was completely filled with Buddhas, all of whom were seen surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣu-saṃghas.
He saw [the Buddha] everywhere throughout hundreds of thousands of locations and villages.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana was once again struck with great wonder and doubt;

after reflecting further, he used his divine eye to look toward Uttarakuru and saw the Buddha together with the community of bhikṣus receiving food. He also saw himself among them, as well as the other disciples.
Again, he looked toward Pūrvavideha and saw the Buddha among a great multitude of people preaching the Dharma;
it was likewise in the land of Aparagoyānī, where he saw the World-Honored Buddha sitting in meditation, and countless thousands of beings all saw him and paid homage to the Buddha.
The assembly of disciples also each sat in samādhi and samāpatti according to their respective forms and appearances, and they likewise saw their own bodies within those [forms].
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana became even more filled with doubt and wonder.

Sitting again, he contemplated the deities upon the earth; thereupon, he again saw the Buddha together with his assembly of disciples, and he also saw himself among them along with the other disciples. Likewise, he saw the deities in the midst of space, and that the Buddha was therein preaching the Dharma for hundreds of thousands of countless devas dwelling in the sky, while he also saw himself and the assembly of disciples within it.

In this manner, he surveyed the first heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Suyāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and up to the Brahmā Heaven. Furthermore, he saw the Buddha in the Brahmā Heaven, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of Brahmās, preaching the Dharma to them; he also saw his own physical form and appearance, as well as all members of the assembly, each exactly like Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The supernormal powers, transformations, and activities performed by all were likewise identical, and he saw himself among them preaching the Dharma for everyone, just as Maudgalyāyana did.
Furthermore, he transformed all those in the assembly so that they were each like the bhikṣu Śāriputra, emitting the radiance of wisdom and uttering the lion’s roar within the great multitude.
In this manner, each one, by means of their own power of wisdom, expounded the Dharma for the Great Disciples.

Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was struck with such terror that his hair stood on end; yet, filled with great wonder and leaping for joy, he gave rise to a virtuous mind and exclaimed three times in self-praise:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are truly most marvelous; their unimpeded conduct and their deeds are also most marvelous.
Greatly moved, he attained a state of joy and leaped for gladness; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he praised them, saying:
"Homage to the Buddha!"

At that time, a great sound was heard, and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven trembled; thereupon, incalculable hundreds of thousands of devas gathered together and, arriving at the place where the Buddha was, addressed him, saying:
"O World-Honored One! "
"For what cause and condition does this great sound exist, shaking the earth to such an extent?
Such is my question,
Tathāgata!"
The Buddha said,
“It is so, O Devaputra!
Because Mahāmaudgalyāyana leaped for joy and took refuge in the Buddha, the Great Earth, prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he moved it to such an extent!”
The Buddha said,
“It is so, O Devaputra!
This bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana shall come in person to inquire about this.”

The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat and went quickly to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then stood before the Buddha with his ten fingers joined in salutation.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"The power he upholds is beyond measure; The Buddha has already attained it.
As the World Hero acts, He is inconceivable."
Having abandoned the three stains and with mind and intellect fully disciplined,
O Honored One among gods and humans!
You are worthy of all offerings.
Though there may be hundreds of thousands of suns filling the void of space, the blind see nothing; the blind receive no light.
When the One of Ten Powers emits radiance, his disciples behold it through its power.
All the disciples cannot equal the Buddha’s brilliance.
Born blind from the womb, they have no sight; the conduct of the disciples is likewise so!
They cannot know the Buddha’s wisdom, nor can they uphold it.
Though one may have faith and accept these teachings of the Tathāgata,
there is nothing therein that can truly know the conduct of the Honored One;
it is like wishing to compare the water in a cow’s footprint to the great ocean.
His virtue is like Mount Sumeru, yet it is compared to a mustard seed;
Like the radiance of the sun, how could it be equated with a firefly?
The virtue of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, cannot be matched by his disciples.
One cannot compare Mount Sumeru to a mustard seed;
nor can the radiance of the sun and moon be compared to the light of a firefly;
nor can it be compared to the water in a cow’s footprint, for it cannot be likened to the great ocean.
To compare them to a disciple is not to treat them as Bodhisattvas;
it would be like comparing a blind man to one with sight,
or like comparing a beggar to a Cakravartin!
Just as the light of the moon is compared to the constellations,
so too the virtues of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, cannot be matched by his disciples.
While he wanders among human beings, he further manifests upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
All manifestations are like illusions, yet all receive his blessings and protection.
Unaware that the Buddha was there, I thought the world was empty;
I shall no longer behold the Buddha, nor the community of bhikṣus.
Within this palace, I always dwell and sit;
for the sake of the celestial maidens, I perform the work of instructing them and preaching the Dharma.
Then, by means of my divine eye, I survey Jambudvīpa.
He then beheld all the hundreds of kingdoms, regarding them as lands devoid of merit.
Contemplating this world, he immediately saw the World-Honored One at Rājagṛha,
partaking of a meal together with his disciples.
Within the royal palace of King Piṃśa, Dwelling amidst the great halls;
Together with the gathered assembly, Surrounded by his retinue,
There he beheld the Buddha, Like gazing upon a mountain of ice and snow.
He saw himself as Maudgalyāyana, stationed to the left of the Buddha;
he also saw Śāriputra,
attending to the Buddha on his right.
And furthermore, including all other disciples as well;
I myself recall calling upon the Buddha, who descended to Jambudvīpa and then returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven— the Buddha remained in that very place.
Thereupon, looking inward with clarity, he saw himself dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
reflecting further with discernment, he found himself situated in Jambudvīpa.
And once again, he beheld the World-Honored One!
He was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī;
seated amidst the great assembly, he extensively preached the Dharma to all.
Furthermore, he saw himself within that great gathering.
Furthermore, Śāriputra! You shall see him,
together with his disciples,
manifesting among the Śākya clan and appearing to go on almsround.
He is seen in Vaiśālī, receiving alms from the people;
he appears dwelling in Vārāṇasī, walking in and out;
wherever he may be, his body is seen everywhere.
Now appearing in Uttarakuru, together with the assembly of his disciples,
he wanders about for alms and beholds Lake Anavatapta.
He likewise appears there now, together with the assembly of his disciples.
They all sat together and ate.
Furthermore, I saw the World-Honored One manifesting his arrival in Aparagoyānī, and again being present in Pūrvavideha.
For the sake of countless koṭis, he expounds their meaning.
Behold for yourselves, Maudgalyāyana!
He performs transformations there.
Manifesting his own supernormal powers, he reveals to people his original practice.
Thereupon, the earth deities behold his dwelling place;
the celestial deities in the void perform for him the rites of the Dharma.
He has fully revealed them all, so that we now behold this unsurpassed Dharma;
in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, he preaches the True Dharma for all,
and what is seen in the Yāma Heaven is likewise exactly thus!
I see him in the Tuṣita Heaven, and likewise in the Māra Heaven;
he appears in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
I see all his disciples, as well as the World-Honored One himself!
Abiding in the Brahma heavens, what he sees is likewise so!
For the sake of the many koṭis of Brahmas, he preaches the Dharma for them all.
Thereupon, he sees his own body pervading everywhere among those Brahmas;
All other disciples, their entire assembly was likewise so.
All that the Buddhas of the past had practiced was also thus:
their walking paths and trees, as well as their niches and places of rest.
Thereupon they all beheld countless Kings of Dharma;
such as these were their likenesses, all like the Lion of the Śākyas!
While I was here in this place, what I saw was truly most marvelous.
Among all the dharmas and deeds I have seen, none are more magnificent than this.
O World-Honored Ones, the Buddhas!
How wondrous is the emission of your radiance!
He then performed such transformations, the most honored among those with supernormal powers.
While remaining in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he preached the Dharma without coming or going;
yet throughout Jambudvīpa, he was seen everywhere.
In kingdoms, cities, and districts, in villages and other places,
they constantly praise [the Buddha] equally and preach the Dharma for them.
As I behold it, all these are the World-Honored Ones!
And he saw all his disciples, who had each attained tranquil concentration:
Mahākauṣṭhila and Kauṣṭhila, as well as Revata;
Kātyāyana and Pūrṇa, together with Mahākāśyapa.
I have already beheld the tracks of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
praised by countless beings, hearing of them is like the ocean.
Thereupon, I saw myself entirely within them; my body was present in every one of them.
With boundless virtues, their assembly is thus!
Such a great sound as this arises from the summit of Mount Sumeru;
for this reason, I pay homage to the World-Honored One!
His virtue is inconceivable;
in terror, we seek refuge in him, our hair standing on end.
Now we wish to prostrate ourselves with our five limbs, bowing our heads and faces in homage.
Such a great sound pervades everywhere, reaching all without exception;
this entire trichiliocosm is shaken by its great trembling.
Standing upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, he radiates forth vast, great light.
I too remained there and beheld them all completely.
Stricken with fear at this, I hastened to the place where the Buddha was;
arriving there immediately, I stood before the Honored One among Men!
And they asked concerning this Dharma, their hearts filled with fear and wonder:
"What practices must be performed to be able to bring about such transformations?"
What constitutes the work of a Buddha?
I pray that you will explain this for me.
Thus it is in Jambudvīpa; it is likewise in the heavens above.
In the east, south, west, and north, it is thus in all four directions;
even if one were in the Brahma-heaven, it would be the same in empty space!
I myself call this "possessing virtue," and bestowing blessings is what I call "benefit."
When I relied on my own attainment of the Way, my supernormal powers were peerless.
Yet my seeking was so excessive that it scorched the very root of the Way;
I fell away from the conduct of the Tathāgata and became distant from the Buddha’s wisdom.
Thereupon he reflected to himself: "This mind has no liberation;
its original nature must be thus, yet I have resolved to seek the Buddha-way.
Now, repentance brings no benefit, for my practice is entirely exhausted."
When all the sense-faculties are completely severed, they are of no benefit to the Buddha-dharma.
It is like a person who enters the sea to seek and gather various treasures;
having abandoned the *maṇi* jewel, they do not take it, but instead seek out mud and mire.
Examining myself as well as others,
I see that you have abandoned the conduct of the World-Honored One to instead seek the path of the disciples.
If there is doubt or indolence, such practice will not lead to Buddhahood.
Exerting diligence to give rise to the aspiration for the Way, one unites all virtuous qualities.
By practicing such diligent austerities, one may transcend the three realms;
if one can perform such deeds, the wisdom of a Buddha can be swiftly attained.
I pray that you will bow your head in homage and take refuge in all the World-Honored Ones!
Those who have attained this and uphold the most supreme wisdom of the Buddha are able to manifest infinite transformations; such a one exists alone: the Lion of the Śākyas!
"For all who see or hear this, their doubts shall be forever removed.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"It is within your own sphere of activity that you are thus able to look upon and behold."
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

Just as the realm of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is inconceivable, such that even if all humans and crawling insects were to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha and gather together to collectively deliberate and investigate it, they would still be unable to know or see it; how much less could you, a single disciple, hope to calculate and understand it?
If one cannot even know what is done in a single place, how much less can one wish to know the realm of the Buddha?
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!

Furthermore, when future generations gather together, having assembled, they sit in one place and observe the transformations of the Path. Such are the transformations manifested by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through his supernormal powers; these are called the transformations of the Path, the transformations of supernormal power, and the infinite transformations, as described in the words of the Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana then said: "So it is,
World-Honored One!"

When the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had heard what the Buddha had said, he saw himself upon a lotus flower, emitting light from his body while in the Brahma heaven; speaking there from that very place, his words were heard throughout the four continents.
Thereupon Maudgalyāyana spoke in verse:
“The appearance of a Buddha in the world Is exceedingly difficult to encounter;
It occurs but once in countless hundreds of thousands of millions Of incalculable koṭis of kalpas.”
Just as the udumbara flower is extremely difficult to encounter, so too is a Buddha difficult to see;
yet the World-Honored One surpasses even that.
He is like a sovereign king, a flying Cakravartin.
Always possessing supernormal powers, his strength of merit was likewise so!
His sons numbered a thousand, and they were fully endowed with the seven treasures;
they went to where the Buddha was to listen to and receive the words of the supreme Dharma.
Brahmā and Śakra!
You shall obtain mastery over all that you desire;
whether you wish to delight in the heavens or take pleasure in the human world.
Delighting oneself with the five pleasures, indulging the mind in joy and merriment;
yet if one goes to the presence of the Dharma King, all wishes may be attained.
If one is able to renounce and leave behind all cravings and desires, [one shall find true peace].
Reaching the tranquility of nirvāṇa is like tasting the flavor of ambrosia.
Those who wish to attain the ultimate and obtain the most sublime power of spiritual faculties should go to where the Hero of the World dwells and listen to the words of the supreme Dharma.
Whether there be Pratyekabuddhas or their various disciples—
among all those who possess two feet, the Buddha is the most supreme and honored.
Having subdued the Māra King, along with all his officials and retinues,
you shall go to the Tathāgata and behold the Lord of Dharma!

Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana inspired countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devaputras from the desire realm and the form realm to hasten, each bringing their own celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial unguents, celestial ornaments, and celestial perfumes. Carrying these all together, they went to where the Buddha was; each took these flowers as an offering and scattered them over the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana, having gathered the assembly of devas together in one place by means of his supernormal power, went to where the Buddha was; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and then withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha spoke to Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Maudgalyāyana!
Listen as I explain the discourse on the infinite dharmas of the divine transformations of the spiritual powers."
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana received the instruction and listened.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

A trichiliocosm consists of ten billion suns and moons, ten billion great oceans, ten billion Mount Sumerus, and ten billion sets of four continents; this is called a 'trichiliocosm,' constituting a single buddha-field."
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
Would one call a single Jambudvīpa "I have attained enlightenment within this"?
Maudgalyāyana!
Do not view it in this way. Why is that?
Maudgalyāyana!

Throughout all four continents, he preaches the Dharma according to their respective aspirations—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and he knows who shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who is in the mother’s womb, who is in the Tuṣita Heaven, and who has entered *parinirvāṇa*; he knows all these things.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
To the east of this trichiliocosm, beyond these four continents, there are twelve thousand four-continental worlds.
In that world-system of four continents, named *Vimalā*, there is a Buddha titled *Vairocanamati*—
translated into the Jin language as "Mirror-like Clarity and Stainless"— who is currently dwelling and preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
The people of that world of four continents are free from lust, anger, and delusion; they constantly draw near to the Dharma and the Path, delighting in hearing, receiving, and practicing it.
Among them, those who seek the Bodhisattva path are few, while those who seek the path of a Pratyekabuddha are even fewer, and those who seek the practice of a Śrāvaka are extremely numerous.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

In that Buddha’s [teaching, which is like a mirror bright and stainless], for every single Dharma he preached, ninety-nine billion people understood the Vehicle of the Disciples (śrāvakayāna). In that realm, the four virtues of a śramaṇa were not taught; thus, they did not hear the teaching of the four virtues of a śramaṇa."
"What are the four virtues?
They are the srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, and the arhat.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!"

The people of that world, while remaining in a single sitting, all attained the realization of the six supernormal powers and reached the eight stages of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Each, knowing for themselves that they were liberated from birth and death, leaped with joy into the air at a height of seven *zhang* above the ground. Seated in mid-air, they entered *parinirvāṇa*; fire issued from within their bodies and consumed them, leaving neither bones nor ashes—nothing at all remained.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
That Buddha currently dwells preaching the Dharma; he delivers beings in tranquility and enters parinirvāṇa in tranquility.

In that world there is neither grasping nor giving; if one feels hunger or thirst, whatever food or drink one thinks of appears naturally before one. Clothing and ornaments are like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Whether arising or ceasing, whether being born, it is not produced from the womb of a woman; there are no women, for they are born spontaneously through the power of merit.
That ground is entirely of golden hue.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
In the land of that Buddha-Tathāgata, the lifespan of the people is five hundred years, though there are some who live longer and some who live shorter.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?"
“Can you know that Buddha (the Tathāgata Vimalaprabhāsasphaṭikaviśuddha)?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I do not know.”
“The Tathāgata of that land is none other than myself!
It is I who teach and guide there by means of the Dharma.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!”
Such as these are called the infinite transformations of the divine power of the Way (*mārgarddhi*); all disciples (*śrāvaka*) and *pratyekabuddhas* are entirely surpassed by them.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!..."

Thereupon, in the southern direction of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of eighteen thousand four-world systems from here, there is a world named Ratanasampadā—which in the language of Jin means "Possession of Jewels.

In that world there are three treasures (gold, silver, and crystal). In that world, the Buddha is named Ratanaketu—which in the language of Jin means "Jewel Banner"—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
Furthermore, that Buddha-Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for those practicing as pratyekabuddhas; in that Buddha-world, bodhisattvas and śrāvakas are few.
When that practitioner passes away from that land, he will be born in a realm where there is no Buddha; in that place, he shall all become pratyekabuddhas.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
"Do you know that Buddha (the Tathāgata Ratnākara, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha)?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "I do not."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"It is I myself!"
In that place, I preach the Dharma to instruct and guide people; this is called the transformation of the supreme power of the divine foot of the Path.
All disciples and pratyekabuddhas remain very far from the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

To the west of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of twenty-two thousand four-continental-system worlds from these four continents, there is a world named Rocaṇacitta—which in the Jin language means 'Jewel-Mind.
In that world, there are seven treasures (gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, red pearl, and musaragalva; these constitute the seven treasures)."

Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana! In that world, the trees are made of jewels; the places for walking meditation are all made of jewels; there are jeweled canopies and jeweled railings, all adorned and embellished with various kinds of gems. There are jeweled bathing pools containing water of eight flavors; food and drink are all spontaneous, arriving naturally as soon as one thinks of them. Just as the clothing and food of the devas in the Tuṣita Heaven, so too are those of the people in that land!
In that land, the name "woman" is never heard, nor is a woman ever seen;
there are no women who give birth with suffering,
nor is there any union between men and women.
Furthermore, they do not indulge in lustful excesses regarding sensual desires;
nor do they indulge in lustful excesses regarding wealth;
nor do they indulge in lustful excesses regarding indolence and arrogance.
Nor are they born from a womb;
all the people in that world are born there through transformation from within the matrix of lotuses,
Maudgalyāyana!
Furthermore, in the world-system called Ratnamati, there is a Buddha named Ratnasama, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who teaches the Dharma there.

That Buddha-Tathāgata speaks of nothing else, but solely through the "Casket of the Bodhisattvas" causes all beings to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he causes incalculable asaṃkhyeya persons to all attain the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, and further, incalculable asaṃkhyeya persons all receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that they shall become Anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddhas.

In that Buddha-world, there are no followers of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles; all are bodhisattvas. Furthermore, there is no affection or craving, nor do they harbor such thoughts, as these qualities fill the four continents of that world-system.
The Tathāgata of that land has a lifespan of eighty-four thousand years;
the people of that land have lifespans likewise, though some are longer and some shorter.
When the lifespan of those people ends, they do not fall into the three evil realms, nor are they born in the borderlands.

When the bodhisattvas in that land reach the end of their lifespan, they are reborn with even greater purity in pure buddha-fields, where they behold the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, face to face!
Among those devas, nāgas, and gandharvas, their minds do not harbor thoughts of inequality or distinction; all possess the intention for sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

Although the devas, nāgas, and gandharvas all share these names and aspire to the same goal, and although their various forms of knowledge are equalized by means of supreme wisdom, whether they be devas, nāgas, gandharvas, or humans, they should always be devoted to wisdom.
"In this regard, Maudgalyāyana, what do you think?
Do you know that those jewels and so forth have a Tathāgata currently present there preaching the Dharma?
Maudgalyāyana said:
“It cannot compare,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"That Buddha was none other than my own self; it was I who, in that place, taught and guided by means of the Dharma.
Such as this is called the transformation of the infinite power of the divine foot of the Way."
This is not something that can be known or reached by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
To the north of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of thirty-six thousand four-continental worlds from this world-system of four continents, there is a world named Fearless."
That world possesses two treasures (gold and silver).
In that Buddha-world, there are no bodies of hell-beings, no bodies of animals, and no hungry ghosts; nor do beings fear being born in the borderlands.
Among them, there is no one who has violated the precepts; nor do they disparage what they have seen;
nor do they violate their lineage;
nor do they place any faith or conviction in other paths or in the Nirgranthas.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
In the world-system called Vigatabhaya, there dwells a Buddha named Vigatatrāsa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is preaching the Dharma there."
That Buddha-Tathāgata then proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree. Having reached the foot of the Bodhi tree, seventy-two billion nayutas of Māras approached his location.
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested himself as a bodhisattva seeking the Way who had not yet attained sarvajñatā;
at that moment, the Māras then conjured seventy-two billion nayutas of trees.
At that time, the Bodhisattva also manifested seventy-two billion nayutas of bodhisattvas, each sitting beneath a tree that had been created for them.
Then Māra was terrified and greatly astonished, thinking to himself: "What is this?"
When this Bodhisattva examined the matter, he wished to pull [the phantom] out from that seat.
At that time, the emanated Bodhisattvas spoke to the phantom created by Māra:
"Just as you and all the hosts of Māras are, so too are all dharmas; why then do you ask 'where'?"
"Who is this Bodhisattva that you wish to drag out?

While I have been here in meditative reflection and contemplation, I have constantly generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* according to the merits I have previously and subsequently performed, and I have exhorted others to resolve their minds and seek the Bodhisattva path. Why do you, lacking any intention to provide encouragement or assistance, instead wish to drag me out?"
The Bodhisattva, in meditative concentration, reflected:
"If the evil deeds I have committed do not naturally vanish simply because I do not encourage others to seek bodhisattvahood, why should I even attempt to drag them along with me?"
"For this reason, you are unable to lead him away; do not cause yourself harm by acting thus.
Thereupon, Māra again asked the Bodhisattva:
"How much merit have you cultivated to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and how are you able to exhort others to seek the path of a bodhisattva?"
He replied, "O Māras!

Suppose there were as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges, and one were to fill them all with precious jewels and offer them as a gift; [yet this merit would not equal that of one who hears this Dharma]."
To uphold this resolve for the Way, the merit one produces exceeds even that! Furthermore, O Māras!

Suppose worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with all people, and one were to bestow upon them all things that bring peace, serving them with reverence for a thousand kalpas; if one were to take the merit and blessings from such deeds and apply them toward seeking the Way—[this would still not equal the merit of upholding the resolve for the Way].
The Māra asked again:
"Your meritorious deeds are indeed such as these!
But as for those who seek out the faults of a bodhisattva, what would their transgression be?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"As you have said, if all those people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to be sought out and their eyes were all gouged out—would the sin committed thereby not be very great?"
The Māra replied,
"Very many.
The Bodhisattva said to the Māra:
"If one were to lead away a bodhisattva, the sin would be many times greater than this, for it would be to lead away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, seventy-two billion nayutas of Māra’s hosts, through these skillful means and having witnessed these transformations, all gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, all the bodhisattvas who had resolved their minds [for enlightenment] took celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial unadorned flowers, and celestial fragrant ointments, and scattered them over the bodhisattva. They also offered and delighted the bodhisattva with a thousand kinds of celestial music, the sounds of which all proclaimed:
"May the Teacher of the Three Realms quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the supreme perfect enlightenment!"
Having offered this praise, he then saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree, having already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the supreme perfect enlightenment.
Thereupon, another hundred thousand devaputras thought to themselves:

"Now that these hosts of Māras have come here, they shall no longer enter the three evil realms; they shall also attain liberation and will surely give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Thereupon, Vigatabhaya-dāna said:
"Now that you have attained Buddhahood, you shall therefore be named Tathāgata Vigatabhaya!
For what reason is this name given?"
"I shall give the gift of fearlessness.
When he had thus spoken these words regarding the granting of fearlessness, all worlds came to know that the Buddha had attained the Way.
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Maudgalyāyana!
That Tathāgata Fearless Giver of the World was none other than myself."
In that world, I instruct them by means of the Dharma.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
This is called the Tathāgata’s transformation through the infinite power of the divine foot of the Path; it cannot be sustained by any of the disciples or pratyekabuddhas.
The Sutra on the Buddha’s Exposition of the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Foot-Powers, Scroll Three;
The Sutra on the Buddha’s Exposition of the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Foot-Powers, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin Dynasty.

"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana! To the southeast of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of eighty-four thousand four-continent worlds from this land, there is a world named Samantaprabhā (in the language of Jin, 'Pervasive Equality').
The Buddha there is named Citta-kūṭa-tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha (in the language of Jin:)."
The Tathāgata Māyāpuṣpa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.

That world-system of four continents is exceedingly beautiful; throughout the eighteen streets and alleys in the east, west, south, and north, precious jewels cover the ground. It is as soft as celestial raiment, and from the earth grow supple grasses four inches high. All that exists upon that ground consists of various distinct colors, which are spread everywhere in this manner.
When they walk and set foot upon the ground, the grass is everywhere soft and pleasing; when the foot is lifted, it grows back as before, and the ground is level throughout like the palm of a hand.
Maudgalyāyana!
It is thus throughout all these worlds.
There is a city named Bhadrayasas, which in the language of Jin means "Virtuous Honored One."

The people within that city lived in peace, security, abundance, prosperity, and great joy; it was thirty-two yojanas long from east to west and twelve yojanas wide from south to north, such as this, Maudgalyāyana!
All the people of that noble city of Śobhavatī dwell together therein.
The population of that kingdom is so vast and numerous that it exceeds the number of people in Aṅga, Magadha, and Kośala combined.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!

That Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Illusory Flower (Māyāpuṣpa), dwells and travels within the city of Śubhavarṇa; there, in a single assembly, he preaches the Dharma with a lion’s roar, causing thirty koṭis of people to all attain arhatship, and another thirty koṭis of people to attain the stage of anāgāmin.
Furthermore, thirty nayutas of people attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
another thirty nayutas of people attained the stage of Srotāpanna;
and another thirty nayutas of people resolved upon the practice of Pratyekabuddhahood.
Furthermore, twice as many incalculable beings resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
additionally, another incalculable number of people all performed meritorious deeds.
Maudgalyāyana!
In that world of four continents, there is a tree named Matu-sa-pi (in the Jin language:
"this tree is like honey"). Its flowers, fruits, and seeds are always present without deficiency, and the flavor of its flowers, fruits, and seeds is like food and drink of a hundred flavors.

Whether they be men or women, if they desire a single flower or a single fruit, they may obtain it and eat it; they will be at peace and fully satisfied, remaining without hunger or weakness for seven days. Their complexion will not fade, their bodies will be healthy, robust, and agile, and they will possess vigor. Having finished eating this, it is as if they have consumed ambrosia; furthermore, there will be no urination, no defecation, and no spitting of mucus or saliva.

There were no farmers to cultivate the fields, nor were there any merchants to lend or repay debts; all within that land ate together from these flowers and fruits. From the beginning, that country knew nothing of poverty or wealth; all were equal and without distinction.

"Maudgalyāyana! That Tathāgata in that world has a community of ninety-six billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of disciples, and the assembly of bodhisattvas is twice as large as the number of disciples."
There is a garden named Samantakūṭa— translated into the Jin language as "Dharma Garden"—
which contains various fruits.
The assembly of disciples always sits within this garden for their meals and drinks.

The assembly of his disciples and the assembly of bodhisattvas all sat beneath the trees; when they wished to eat, the trees would naturally sway, causing flowers and fruits to fall, and those that fell all landed within their alms bowls.
When they have finished eating and drinking, the trees do not shake and the flowers and fruits do not fall, remaining exactly as they were before.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
All things in that world exceed this world many times over and are beyond measure.
Maudgalyāyana!
The Tathāgata of that world is none other than myself;
it is I who instruct and guide them in that world through the Dharma.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
This is called the transformation of the Tathāgata’s infinite spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), which all disciples and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

To the southwest of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of seventy-four world-systems of four continents from this world-system of four continents, there is a world named Pi-shih-p'an-tien (比實颰填), which in the language of Jin means 'Receptive' (Rongshou).
There were eighty thousand kings; in each kingdom there were eighty thousand cities, and outside each city there were eighty thousand villages.
The domains ruled by these eighty thousand kings consisted of eighty thousand cities and eighty-four thousand smaller towns.

In every city, village, town, small city, and *krośa*, all were filled with hundreds of thousands of them; those kings all practiced the Dharma, and all unrighteous matters were completely eliminated.
Each of these kings had eighty-four thousand wives and court ladies.
At that time, the court ladies were of such exquisite beauty as to be the most supreme in the world.
Each king had five hundred crown princes, and each king had twelve thousand daughters.
These twelve thousand women were all beautiful, the most excellent in the world.
The laws of these kings involved neither whips nor staves, nor did they possess weapons; each of these kings governed his own kingdom through self-discipline.
Maudgalyāyana!
In that world named Saṃvartanīya, there is a Buddha named Prabhūtaratnadhvaja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—in the language of Jin [Chinese]:
the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna-prabhāsa, the One Free from Attachment, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One—who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.

"Maudgalyāyana, when that Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he leaped into the air above those four continents and sat cross-legged at a height of seven fathoms from the ground; with each cross-legged posture, he emitted a great radiance."

At that time, the worlds of the four continents all became visible to one another; celestial flowers rained down, and all musical instruments sounded spontaneously without being struck, each instrument producing hundreds of thousands of melodies. The earth shook in six ways, and the sounds of the various musical performances were like the voice of Brahmā, brought about by the merit of countless hundreds of thousands of deeds performed.

He turned the wheel of Dharma; all defilements of desire were completely exhausted, and he attained *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Upholding what the Bodhisattva knew, he preached the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.

"When that Tathāgata preached the Dharma, throughout this world-system of four continents, the eighty thousand kings, along with their consorts, court ladies, sons, and daughters, having witnessed the Buddha’s transformations, all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
All the people in that land—men and women, sons and daughters—were all distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
These kings, along with their consorts, court ladies, sons, and daughters, requested ordination as śramaṇas from the Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata granted permission for them all to become śramaṇas.

Having become a śramaṇa, wherever he dwelt—whether in cities, towns, villages, or settlements—at every place he reached, he always traveled on foot and did not ride in carriages or on horses. He constantly stayed in monasteries for his sleep, rising, eating, and drinking; he no longer engaged in farming or planting, but ate only what was provided spontaneously, as devas and humans descended to provide him with all his offerings.

"At that time, when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for a second assembly, all the disciples and practitioners attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, and all the bodhisattva practitioners attained the Receptive Patience of Joy."
During the third assembly’s preaching of the Dharma, all people attained the stage of Anāgāmin, and those practicing as Bodhisattvas all attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

During the fourth assembly’s preaching of the Dharma, all attained Arhatship, and those practicing as Bodhisattvas all attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); likewise, the ladies of the court, the palace maidens, and both men and women all attained the patience of non-arising.
At that time, the queen, the court ladies, and all the women transformed their female bodies and all attained male bodies; they no longer appeared in female forms.
Then, that Tathāgata bestowed upon them all the prediction of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
Do you know that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaprabhāsvara in that land?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“It is beyond me,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"It is none other than this very body!
This is called the transformation of the Tathāgata’s infinite spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana!"
This is beyond the reach of knowledge of all disciples and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
To the northwest of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of fifty-five thousand four-continent worlds from here, there is a world named Gandhavatī (in the Jin language: [Gandhavatī])."
As for its fragrance, that world is entirely composed of *ulakaśara* sandalwood; even a piece of this sandalwood as large as a single coin is worth the price of an entire world.
In that world there are trees called *samantagandha*—in the language of Jin, "its fragrance universally perfumes."

In that world, each tree emits a fragrance that extends for four hundred *li*. The ground is entirely covered with lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels; each flower has hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of petals in countless colors, and the flowers are as soft and supple as celestial silk.
Flowers grow there two zhang high; their fragrance pervades the four continents of the world, being most exquisite.
In that world, the four continents have canopies of *candana* sandalwood, and even the walking paths are made of *candana*. *Pundarika* lotuses appear on both sides.
That world has no cities, districts, or villages; it is covered only by canopies of interlaced jewels.
The food and drink of the people of that world are like those of the fifth heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Furthermore, that land emits fragrances that universally perfume the world; the Buddha there is named Gandhamukhara (in the language of Jin:
Fragrance-Emitting Radiance) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.

In that Tathāgata’s world, the practice consists solely of bodhisattvas; there are no followers of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha vehicles. That world is entirely filled with those who possess supernormal powers (ṛddhi), and all those bodhisattvas have attained inconceivable patience (akṣayākṣānti).
Among those bodhisattvas, there was a bodhisattva named Sarvadharmāparigrahavyūha (in the Jin language: *Yīqièfǎ wújí jījù*), who had attained inconceivable matters through his vows;

he had already attained the three patiences (*kṣānti*) and reached mastery in the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). His responses were all superior to others, and he had made offerings to incalculable numbers of Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
Regarding all those dharmas that have no ultimate accumulation, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
'I now wish to question the Buddha; if he is willing to speak, I shall ask him.'"

Having formed this thought, he rose from his seat and emitted light from every single pore of his body that illuminated four hundred *li*. The radiance from his body pervaded the entire realm; hundreds of thousands of kinds of flowers appeared in countless colors, each exceedingly fresh and beautiful. These flowers remained in the air at a height of seven fathoms above the ground, and he mentally resolved to take them as an offering.

At that moment, from within the void, the sound of gentle music was heard, like celestial music; these musical sounds all issued forth the sounds of the eight seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*). From each sound of a Dharma seal, eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of sūtra scrolls emerged, and seventy-two thousand verses were produced.

At that time, the Bodhisattva leaped up into the air and sat cross-legged; the assembly of ninety-six koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of people all dwelt in the stage of *avaivartika*, all attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, and were destined for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Maudgalyāyana! Such bodhisattvas of such appearance and form fill that world.
Among all its people, there is no one who is blind, nor is there anyone who is mute."
Furthermore, there were none who were lame, none who were deaf, none who were poor, and none who were ugly.

All the people therein were bodhisattvas, possessing the thirty-two marks of a great man. In that world, there were no other miscellaneous or heterodox practices; nor was there any need for food or drink in that land, as they took the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance.
In that land, there are no people of mixed races such as Qiang, Lu, Yi, or Di;
nor are there the three evil realms;
nor are there any border regions.
"Nor do they pass away from that place to be reborn in another land; rather, if there is one who passes away and ceases, they immediately attain the state of a Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Maudgalyāyana!"
The Tathāgata of that world is none other than my own self!

In that land, I instruct and transform beings through the Dharma; this is called the transformation of the ultimate power of the divine feet of the Way, which no disciples or pratyekabuddhas can fathom or know.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
To the northeast of this trichiliocosm, forty-two thousand four-continent worlds away, there is a world named Udumbara (in the language of Jin:
Yingshi).

The people of that world have excessive lust; they are full of greed, anger, ignorance, stinginess, and clamorous obstinacy. Their faculties are habituated to the depraved; they lack faith, are envious, commit evil, and are full of doubt, malice, and quick temper. They are lazy, indolent, and prone to forgetfulness; they are stubborn and fearless. Clinging to the notions of self, person, and life-span, they lack wisdom. Like wild birds and beasts, they know no shame or modesty; they possess no propriety, and their minds are deluded and frantic.

That world is hideous in appearance, colorless, and devoid of any sense of propriety; its land consists only of mud and various impurities; life there is arduous and toilful, with food and clothing insufficient; its inhabitants delight in fighting and revile one another.
If it rains once in the sixth month and once again in the year, the five grains will not flourish.

This is caused by evil conduct; the ground of that world is as hard as iron or stone, and its mountains and peaks are uneven, like the thorns of a *kaṇṭaka* plant that wound one's feet when stepped upon. Poisonous evils prevail there, and the earth produces only thorny brambles.

The water produced in that world is turbid, foul, salty, bitter, stinking, and impure; the people drink it, and they clothe themselves entirely in straw and fodder. Destitute and beset by hardship, they look upon one another and take turns serving as each other's laborers.

The king of that world was of a quick temper and constantly prone to anger; the people therein were subjected to immense labor and service, toiling with great hardship to sustain their livelihoods through farming. Yet the king seized all their grain, millet, and wealth, and there was no one who did not suffer the calamity of his violent beatings and punishments.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
Within that realm, the calamities experienced in the present life are as severe as this;
compared to this, they are even many times greater.
When the lifespan of those in that world comes to an end, they all fall into the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
In that world of four continents, the Tathāgata is named Jambukhaṇḍika-londanamaka-kalū (in the Jin language: *Jambukhaṇḍika-londanamaka-kalū*)."
With compassion and pity for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he preached the Dharma for him.

Maudgalyāyana, that Buddha-Tathāgata manifested eighteen great transformations while preaching the Dharma; after seven hundred years of preaching had concluded, not a single person among them had understood the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was neither weary nor fatigued; he preached the Dharma as before, always maintaining great compassion as he expounded it.
Thus it was, Maudgalyāyana!

Whether that Buddha, the World-Honored One, arrived at villages, provinces, districts, or towns, or wandered through them while traveling on foot, there was no place where the people of those lands did not revile him, treat him with contempt, pull at his robes, spit upon him, or speak with anger and malice. Yet the World-Honored One endured all of this, comforting, protecting, and nurturing them, desiring to deliver them and lead them to Nirvāṇa.
Maudgalyāyana!

During all those years, the Tathāgata constantly taught the Dharma to nurture and protect them; while he was teaching the Dharma, eighty-four thousand nayutas of people attained arhatship, and another eighty-four thousand nayutas of people attained the stage of anāgāmin.
Furthermore, eighty-four thousand nayutas of people attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
another eighty-four thousand nayutas of people attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Within a single day, the entire great assembly shaved their hair and beards, became śramaṇas, and all received the full precepts. At that time, both those who were still training and those who were no longer training, having received instruction from the Buddha, were able to abandon all former evils within three months and simultaneously entered parinirvāṇa.

That Buddha is eternally present, further nurturing and protecting the pratyekabuddhas and those practicing as bodhisattvas; yet because of the evil deeds they have committed, they are born in that land and undergo such intense suffering!
"At that moment, they all attained complete liberation.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"What kind of offenses did these bodhisattvas commit to be born in that land?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"There are four dharmas by which bodhisattvas are reborn in that land."
What are the four?
First, they rely on the name of a bodhisattva to seek offerings, yet do not study the deeds of a bodhisattva.
Second, Maudgalyāyana!
First, they are indolent and unable to practice the deeds of a bodhisattva; even when they see them, they are unable to uphold them. Second, Maudgalyāyana!

When a bodhisattva sees another bodhisattva receiving offerings, they become envious and say: [such-and-such]. Third, Maudgalyāyana! When a bodhisattva sees another bodhisattva receiving offerings, they become envious and jealous, saying: [such-and-such].
"Why do you make offerings?
This is to sever the merit of others and treat them with contempt.
Fourth, Maudgalyāyana!
Because Bodhisattvas were unable to guard their body, speech, and mind, they obtained this [retribution].
It is by means of these matters, Maudgalyāyana,
that they are born in that land.
The Buddha said,
“Maudgalyāyana!
That buddha was none other than my own self.”

In that land, I instruct people through the Dharma; this is called the Tathāgata’s infinite transformation through the divine power of expedient means, which cannot be fathomed by disciples or pratyekabuddhas.
It is thus, Maudgalyāyana! In this way,
the Tathāgata performs the work of a Buddha within this trichiliocosm.
Maudgalyāyana!
It is not that those like you have all manifested themselves completely. Why is this?
The disciples are unable to retain it; for this reason, they cannot manifest it all.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
In this trichiliocosm of a hundred koṭis of four-continent worlds, that Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of all beings."

Furthermore, there are worlds of the four continents where [the Tathāgata] preaches the Dharma appearing in the form, image, and attire of Brahmā; in those worlds, the Tathāgata does not go forth from home to shave his hair and beard.
Furthermore, there are those who preach the Dharma appearing in the physical form and attire of Śakra Devānām Indra;
or those who preach the Dharma appearing in the physical form and attire of the Sun Deity King (Sūryadevaputra);
or again, those who preach the Dharma appearing in the physical form and attire of a Cakravartin King.
In this manner, Maudgalyāyana!
Within this trichiliocosm, he preaches the Dharma according to the aspirations of all people; such instances are incalculable.
Furthermore, there are other countless and incalculable Buddha-fields that cannot be known or reached by any of the disciples or pratyekabuddhas.
For example, Maudgalyāyana!

The palaces of the moon and the sun—the celestial deities of the sun and moon each sit within their respective palaces—neither emerging nor entering, yet sitting there they illuminate and behold the world beneath.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not arise from this place, nor does he go to sit there; yet he perceives all incalculable buddha-fields and manifests himself within them all, according to the aspirations of all beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—protecting and sustaining them while preaching the Dharma for them.
Then the worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Which one, truly, is the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
Is it the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or Jambudvīpa, or the celestial palaces, or the trichiliocosm?"
In these four continents and other worlds, the Dharma is being preached; yet among so many worlds, who can be definitively identified as the Buddha?
How should we understand the discourse on the infinite great almsgiving and the robes of the Great Boundary?
How is this known?
Such was the question posed by Maudgalyāyana:
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Regarding what you have asked, are you able to receive and uphold it?
I shall now explain it to you."
“Maudgalyāyana!
It is like a magician who conjures a person, whether male or female; what is there to truly verify as being male or female?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There is nothing that can be scrutinized as real. Why is this?
Because it is produced by the power of illusory spells and arts; therein, there is nothing to be grasped.”
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"By whom was this illusion conjured?
Is this illusion something that can be produced?"
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha, “It may be done,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"In this way, all these dharmas are like illusions and transformations, devoid of any substantiality, yet they function according to their respective activities.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!"
The illusions produced by a magician through his skillful power perform many actions, yet these illusions are all equal and possess no substantiality.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!

The Tathāgata, by means of wisdom, manifests equally throughout all buddha-fields; thus, there is nothing whatsoever that is grasped, yet for the sake of all that is done, he remains eternally equal. To perform the Buddha-work in this manner is why it is called the Great and Infinite *dakṣiṇā*.
Such is the great retribution for these deeds; as it is, Maudgalyāyana!
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are equal and without distinction.
It is thus, Maudgalyāyana!
All phenomena abide eternally in equality;
as all phenomena abide in equality, so too is the realization of the Way!
The Dharma-realm is without support and is not manifold.

Maudgalyāyana! Reflect deeply upon this: the Tathāgata, having extensively and far-reachingly sought the traces of Buddhahood, is able to manifest as many Tathāgatas with the thirty-two marks as there are sands on the banks of the Ganges, all equal and without distinction. He can also cause them to preach the Dharma through sixty kinds of congregational matters, their speech being identical in tone. All these Tathāgatas fully know the mental activities of all people;

all these Tathāgatas fully know all those who shall attain liberation. They seal the six sense-faculties with the Seal of Liberation and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to gradually attain the fulfillment of wisdom.
These Tathāgatas manifest and preach the Dharma for all beings; all who hear it practice it accordingly, and they equally realize that all sufferings are exhausted.
These Tathāgatas possess three modes of transformation in their preaching of the Dharma, teaching with equal clarity from four directions.
These Tathāgatas fully manifest all the works of a Buddha.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
Among all those Buddhas, which one is truly the holder?
Since the Tathāgata is an illusion and illusions are illusory, what is it that the Tathāgata holds?
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“In this regard, there is no one who can know or uphold it. Why is that?”

Just as with a Tathāgata, so too regarding what a Tathāgata does, there is neither increase nor decrease; for a Tathāgata, there is no manifold activity—whether it be form, or image, or retribution, or wisdom, or supernormal powers, or preaching the Dharma, or the liberation of all people.
"So it is, Tathāgata!
Regarding these manifold matters, one cannot speak of them in various ways.
So it is, Maudgalyāyana!"
It is as you have done! It is as you have seen: all phenomena are likewise like transformations and illusions.
Therefore, all phenomena have no sustainer and no diversity.
“In this way, Maudgalyāyana!
Just as one knows the various parts of a magical illusion, so too should one know all phenomena!
Ordinary people cannot even produce a fraction [of such transformations], let alone the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones!”
Why is this? Maudgalyāyana!

Because all dharmas are practiced as empty, one contemplates with detachment; being without desire or non-desire, whether existent or non-existent, one abides therein. What is performed and what is done is as that which is attained; within the dharma-realm, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
"Maudgalyāyana!
As is the dharma-realm, so does the Tathāgata see it all, know it all, and awaken to it all.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!"
Suppose the land of Jambudvīpa were filled with people, and the Tathāgata were to manifest and display transformations, appearing either as a Tathāgata or as a community of bhikṣus!
That person, passing from one state to another, does not know whether it is the Tathāgata or the community of bhikṣus.
Let alone those people within Jambudvīpa,
Maudgalyāyana!
Maudgalyāyana! Suppose the four continents were filled with gods, humans, and all classes of crawling and flying creatures— whatever beings might be born there—

and suppose that all those people remained before the Buddha for such a long duration of time in their previous lives, all of them remaining before the Buddha, appearing as Tathāgatas or bhikṣus, yet none of them would know one another.
Furthermore, set aside these four continents, Maudgalyāyana!

Suppose that within this trichiliocosm, all the wriggling and crawling creatures were to fill it entirely, and you were to cause them all to obtain human bodies; having obtained human bodies, you were to cause them all to be equal.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!

Having attained a human body, all who have attained a human body are of one and the same kind; they all manifest as the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus, yet they do not recognize one another as they pass from one to another.
“Maudgalyāyana!
Let alone the people of this trichiliocosm.
It is even so, Maudgalyāyana!”

In the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction—and likewise in the eastern, southern, western, northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir—in all such worlds throughout the ten directions, there are exceedingly many, incalculable realms; may all beings therein universally attain human bodies.
"Once they have attained human bodies, Maudgalyāyana, such persons as these—
being of the same kind as the Tathāgata— I shall cause each and every one of them to become like the Tathāgata, and all shall further become members of the bhikṣu-saṃgha!"
Those of such a kind, passing from one to another, are likewise unable to know this for themselves.
"Set that aside, Maudgalyāyana!
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers—"

As the Tathāgata now sits here, he maintains his Buddha-eye to behold all the Buddha-fields, upholding what the Buddha knows; even if one were to speak for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one could not reach the end of such a number.

In this manner, incalculable Buddha-fields are seen while sitting here; as for those Buddha-fields described by the Tathāgata through parables, even if all beings were made into Pratyekabuddhas, they would be unable to know them, unable to count them, unable to weigh them, and unable to behold them.
Pratyekabuddhas are perpetually unable to know this, let alone their disciples.

For this reason, the Tathāgata perceives and knows them all: such hundreds, such thousands, such hundreds of thousands, such koṭis of hundreds of thousands, such gaṅgākalas, such vibhitas, such āyus, such asaṃkhyeyas, such incalculable numbers, such as many grains of sand in the Ganges, and such incalculable trichiliocosm worlds—all of these, completely filled with them.
"So it is, Maudgalyāyana!
the Buddha said.

"In this way, his counting is without obstruction. He gazes directly with his eyes, looking straight ahead without glancing sideways, nor does he crane his neck to look. Maintaining the singular vision of the Buddha-eye, he sees throughout all the immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, boundless, and limitless lands of the ten directions."
In this manner, one may reckon the Buddha-fields, and the people therein, as well as the classes of crawling and wriggling creatures;
likewise, in this manner, one may reckon all the realms of *sattvas*, which are more numerous than the particles of dust upon the earth.
In this way, all the previous lives of Śakra, which had never before performed such deeds, resulted in him attaining human form; he then caused them all to become Cakravartin kings.
Each of these Cakravartin kings sat individually with their own retinues of officials.
As for one Cakravartin king, all his officials and subjects are exactly like that; the succession of Cakravartin kings is just so!
It is thus, Maudgalyāyana!
All the retinues of the Cakravartin kings throughout the entire world constitute the retinue of a single Cakravartin king.
In this manner and by such analogy, all these become Tathāgatas; their physical forms and appearances are all of one and the same kind.

By such causes and conditions, they all stood before him; each of the Cakravartin kings and their retinues stood before him, and each saw for themselves that there was a Tathāgata and a community of bhikṣus. Each of the Cakravartin kings called out:
"The Tathāgata is here alone!"
That is to say, they all see nothing else; each and every one sees only a single Tathāgata and regards all others as non-existent—and so it is for each and every one!
In this way, for each of the Cakravartin kings and their retinues, every single hair on their bodies was a Tathāgata;
and each Tathāgata was accompanied by his own community of bhikṣus.
Is this not the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s boundless supernatural power (ṛddhi-pāda)?
Those who hear this would not dare, even in their thoughts, to say that this is not the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s boundless display.
If there should arise such a thought, it is truly the work of the Tathāgata’s infinite manifestations and transformations;
it is likewise the work performed by immeasurable wisdom.
“Maudgalyāyana! What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
Suppose I were to establish all these people in the state of a Cakravartin King, granting them such a portion of merit.”
"If all those portions of merit were used to make individuals Cakravartin kings, fully endowed with the seven treasures— would such portions of merit not be very great?
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha,
"Very great, indeed, World-Honored One."
O God among Gods!

If even a single person were to attain this, their merit would be immeasurable; how much more so for as many people as there are—beyond calculation and beyond limit—their abundant peace would surpass all other peace.
The Buddha said:
“Maudgalyāyana!
You should receive and uphold what has been thus spoken, and reflect upon it thoroughly!”

If all these śrāvakas were to become cakravartin kings, the merit they would possess would be exceedingly great; yet it would not equal the merit of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata, surpassing it by incalculable degrees.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Such is the virtue of the Tathāgata; this is the Tathāgata’s great supernormal power, his great portion, and his great capability."
In such a world, my regrets would be of no avail.
Why is this? Because, despite having attained supernatural mastery over all phenomena, I have brought harm upon myself.
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"All those who hear of this Tathāgata’s supreme, great transformation of the divine power of the Way shall all attain great virtue. Should any, having heard it, give rise to a single thought regarding its matters—desiring to seek liberation, desiring to study and reach fulfillment, and desiring to obtain this supreme, great transformation of the divine power of the Way—they shall resolve their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
World-Honored One!
Such people as these should be saluted with the head touching the ground. Why is this so?
Such people will attain this before long; they shall never again fear falling into the three evil realms, nor shall they harbor doubts or engage in such deliberations.
They do not wish for the status of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, or gandharvas, nor do they wish to become Brahmās.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
Having thus heard of the infinite transformations of the divine power of the Way, Maudgalyāyana rose, stood with palms joined, and cried out:
"Homage to the Buddha, the World-Honored One!"
One should pay homage to such people as these upon hearing [this teaching], so that they may swiftly attain their aspirations.

Whether they have yet to resolve to set forth or have already set forth, may all such people attain the boundless state like the boundlessness of a Buddha; may their minds no longer waver therein, be free from hesitation, and no longer doubt or believe [alternatively].
At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors made offerings to the Buddha and, regarding the Dharma, all expressed their aspiration and delight.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of kinds of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, and celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers filled the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

When this discourse on the Dharma was being taught, seventy-two thousand nayutas of devas who had cultivated merit since time immemorial all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and spoke these words:
"In future ages, we shall, before the devas and the people of the world, let out the great lion’s roar, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has roared the lion’s roar today."
At that time, the Devaputra Candra and the Devaputra Candraketu came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If sons or daughters of good family, regarding what is spoken in this ‘Chapter on the Dharma Words,’ should receive it, uphold it, contemplate it, or explain it—expounding it widely within the great assembly—how much merit and virtuous reward shall they obtain?”
The Buddha said to the devaputra:

"Regarding these Three Jewels, if sons or daughters of good family do not sever or forget them, but seek to attain them through these words of the Dharma—whether by upholding them themselves or explaining them to others."

Why is this? Just as when the Son of Heaven hears this Dharma, he does not seek anything from the mind of a disciple, nor does he seek anything from the mind of a pratyekabuddha; his mind is always fixed upon anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Why is this? Because they maintain pure liberation,
O Devaputra!
Having attained the various faculties, one reaches this Dharma-discourse and gives rise to the path and a heart of joy; one has no doubt regarding liberation.
O Son of Heaven!
You should uphold this Dharma-discourse and proclaim it widely, so that the Three Jewels are not interrupted and may remain established.
If one upholds, recites, or explains these words of the Dharma for others, what do you think, O Son of Heaven?
The Three Jewels will not be severed and shall abide eternally.
If there is one who upholds or explains this Dharma, O Devaputra,
how could they not abide without severing their connection to the Triple Gem?

If one were to provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick to a thousand Buddhas throughout a hundred thousand kalpas, would anyone be able to calculate the merit obtained by such a person?
"No, World-Honored One, there is no one capable of knowing it.
The Buddha said:
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Regarding these spoken words of the Dharma, those who possess wisdom and discernment know that this merit is incalculable and without limit.
If anyone should uphold these spoken words of the Dharma and preach them among the assembly, their merit would exceed this, such that no one could calculate it."
Thereupon Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is the name of this discourse on the Dharma?"
"How should it be upheld and practiced?
The Buddha said to Maitreya: "O Maitreya!..."
This Dharma discourse is titled "Spoken in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" (Dhāraṇī); it is also titled "The Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Path" (Dhāraṇī).
I entrust this to you and commit it to your care.
"O Maitreya, you should hold this with careful discernment and explain it fully and with careful discernment within this great assembly. Maitreya!
A sūtra such as this is extremely difficult to hear in the world of Jambudvīpa."
"Thus it is, Maitreya!
It is as I have spoken.

When the Buddha had finished speaking, all were filled with joy. The Moon Devaputra, the Moon-Star Devaputra, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and asura subjects, having heard this with delight and joy, came forward and paid homage to the Buddha.
